_comment: Debugging walkthroughs. Joe matches user phrases against `triggers` (substring/keyword) and returns title + ordered steps + tips. Each guide is a procedure, not a fact.

guides.title: Python: ModuleNotFoundError
steps: Check the exact module name in the error and confirm spelling (case-sensitive).
Confirm which Python is running: `python -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)'`.
Confirm which pip matches it: `python -m pip --version`.
Install into the same interpreter: `python -m pip install <package>`.
If you use a venv, activate it first (e.g. `source .venv/bin/activate`) before installing or running.
If the import is a local file, check `sys.path` and that you're running from the right working directory.
Re-run the script — the error should be gone.
tips: Always use `python -m pip` instead of bare `pip` — it guarantees you're installing for the right interpreter.
If you have multiple Pythons, `which -a python python3` shows all of them.
For local packages, an empty `__init__.py` in the folder can fix discovery.

guides.title: Python: ImportError cannot import name X
steps: Read the full traceback — note both files involved in the import chain.
Check if file A imports B, and B imports A — that's a circular import.
Break the cycle: move the shared symbol to a third module, or do the import inside the function instead of the top of the file.
If not circular, verify the symbol exists in the target module: `python -c 'import target; print(dir(target))'`.
Check installed version: `pip show <package>` — the symbol may have been renamed/removed.
Pin a known-working version: `pip install '<package>==<version>'`.
tips: Lazy import (inside a function) is the easiest fix for stubborn circular imports.
`from x import *` hides what's missing — switch to explicit names to surface the real error.
Check the package's CHANGELOG for renames between versions.

guides.title: Python: TypeError debug strategy
steps: Read the exact TypeError message — it names the operation and the offending type.
Find the line in the traceback. Add `print(type(x), x)` right before it for each variable involved.
If it says 'NoneType', a function probably returned None when you expected a value — check return paths.
If it says 'str' where you expected 'int', cast explicitly: `int(x)` or `str(x)`.
If 'object is not callable', you're using `()` on something that isn't a function — likely a variable shadowing a function name.
If 'object is not iterable', wrap it in a list, or check you didn't forget to call a generator function.
tips: Drop a `breakpoint()` on the failing line to inspect everything live.
Most TypeErrors trace back to one variable being a different type than you assumed.
Type hints + `mypy` catch many of these before runtime.

guides.title: Python: AttributeError debug strategy
steps: Look at the message: 'X has no attribute Y'. Note both X (the object) and Y (the missing attribute).
If X is `NoneType`, a function returned None — trace back to where the object was created.
If Y is misspelled, fix the typo. Use `dir(X)` to list real attributes.
If a method moved or was renamed, check the library version: `pip show <package>`.
If it's your class, confirm `__init__` actually sets `self.Y = ...` before this point.
Add `print(type(X), dir(X))` just before the failing line if you're still stuck.
tips: AttributeError on None almost always means a missing return or a failed lookup upstream.
Some libraries lazy-load — try accessing the parent module first.
`hasattr(obj, 'name')` is a quick safety check.

guides.title: Python: IndentationError / TabError
steps: Open the file in an editor that shows whitespace (VS Code: View > Render Whitespace).
Look at the line in the error — check whether it's tabs or spaces.
Pick one: PEP 8 says 4 spaces. Convert the whole file to spaces.
VS Code: open command palette, run 'Convert Indentation to Spaces'.
Or run: `python -m tabnanny <file.py>` to find inconsistencies.
Re-run the script.
tips: Set your editor to insert spaces for the Tab key project-wide.
Add a `.editorconfig` so the whole team agrees: `indent_style = space, indent_size = 4`.
`autopep8 -i <file.py>` will fix indentation in place.

guides.title: Python: pip install fails
steps: Read the full error — note keywords: SSL, proxy, EACCES, no matching distribution, version solving.
Upgrade pip first: `python -m pip install --upgrade pip`.
If 'no matching distribution', check your Python version supports the package (`python --version`).
If SSL error, check your system time is correct, or try `--index-url https://pypi.org/simple`.
If 'permission denied', use a venv instead of system Python, or add `--user`.
If behind a proxy, set `HTTPS_PROXY` env var or pass `--proxy=http://...`.
If still failing, try `pip install -vvv <pkg>` for verbose logs.
tips: Never use `sudo pip install` — make a venv instead.
Some packages need system libs first (e.g. `libpq-dev` for `psycopg2`).
Apple Silicon: many older wheels are x86 only — try `pip install --pre <pkg>` or build from source.

guides.title: Python: venv won't activate
steps: Confirm the venv exists: `ls .venv/bin` (mac/linux) or `dir .venv\Scripts` (windows).
On bash/zsh: `source .venv/bin/activate`.
On fish: `source .venv/bin/activate.fish`.
On Windows cmd: `.venv\Scripts\activate.bat`.
On Windows PowerShell: `.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1` — may need `Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned`.
Confirm activation: `which python` should now point inside `.venv/`.
If still wrong, delete and recreate: `rm -rf .venv && python -m venv .venv`.
tips: If `which python` doesn't change, your activate script wasn't sourced (it was executed in a subshell).
Some shells need a hash refresh: `hash -r` after activating.
VS Code: select the venv interpreter via 'Python: Select Interpreter' command.

guides.title: Python: version conflict / wrong interpreter
steps: List every Python on PATH: `which -a python python3` (or `where python` on Windows).
Find the one you want: `python3.11 -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)'`.
If using pyenv: `pyenv versions` lists installed, `pyenv local 3.11.4` pins a project.
If using asdf: `asdf list python` then `asdf local python <ver>`.
Create a venv with the right one explicitly: `python3.11 -m venv .venv`.
Activate it and re-run.
tips: Never rely on `python` alone — it can be 2.x, 3.x, or missing depending on OS.
Add a `.python-version` file so pyenv auto-switches when you cd in.
macOS: `python` is unlinked by default — Homebrew installs as `python3`.

guides.title: Python: pytest collects 0 tests
steps: Confirm file naming: files must start with `test_` or end with `_test.py`.
Confirm function naming: functions inside must start with `test_`.
Confirm class naming: classes must start with `Test` and have no `__init__`.
Run with verbose discovery: `pytest --collect-only`.
If running from a subdir, try from the project root or add `conftest.py` to the root.
Check `pytest.ini` / `pyproject.toml` for a restrictive `testpaths` or `python_files` setting.
If imports inside the test fail silently, run `pytest -p no:cacheprovider --tb=short` to surface them.
tips: An empty `conftest.py` in the project root often fixes path-related discovery.
Use `pytest --rootdir=.` to be explicit about where the project starts.
If you renamed a test, pytest's cache might be stale — delete `.pytest_cache/`.

guides.title: Python/Flask: working outside application context
steps: Identify where you're using `current_app`, `g`, `session`, or `url_for` — those need an app context.
If it's in a script (not a request), wrap the code: `with app.app_context(): ...`.
If it's in a CLI command, register it with `@app.cli.command` so Flask provides context automatically.
If it's a background thread/job, push a context manually inside the worker.
For request-time things (`request`), you need a request context, not just app context.
Re-run and confirm the error is gone.
tips: Factory pattern projects: import `current_app` instead of the app instance directly.
Celery tasks: use `flask.app_context` inside the task body, not at module import.
`g` is per-request; don't try to share data across requests with it.

guides.title: Python/Django: migrations broken
steps: Run `python manage.py showmigrations` to see what's applied vs pending.
If 'no changes detected' but you changed a model, ensure the app is in `INSTALLED_APPS`.
Generate: `python manage.py makemigrations <app>`.
Apply: `python manage.py migrate`.
If you hit 'inconsistent migration history', someone deleted a migration that was already applied — recreate it or `migrate <app> zero` then re-migrate (dev only).
If two branches each made migrations, run `python manage.py makemigrations --merge` to create a merge migration.
tips: NEVER edit a migration file that's already applied in production.
`migrate --plan` shows exactly what will run, in order.
For a clean dev reset: drop the DB and re-run `migrate`.

triggers: this event loop is already running
guides.title: Python/asyncio: event loop is already running
steps: Recognize the cause: Jupyter (and some frameworks) already run an event loop, so `asyncio.run()` conflicts.
In Jupyter: just `await your_coroutine()` directly at the top level.
Or install nest-asyncio: `pip install nest_asyncio` then `import nest_asyncio; nest_asyncio.apply()`.
In FastAPI/aiohttp handlers, never call `asyncio.run` inside a handler — `await` instead.
If you genuinely need a fresh loop, use `asyncio.new_event_loop()` in a separate thread.
tips: Jupyter notebooks have an implicit loop — `asyncio.run` will always fail there.
`nest_asyncio` is a duct-tape fix; avoid in production code.
In Python 3.11+, `asyncio.Runner()` gives more control than `asyncio.run`.

triggers: task was destroyed but it is pending
guides.title: Python/asyncio: task pending / coroutine never awaited
steps: Find the warning's filename:line — it's the coroutine that wasn't awaited.
If you called `foo()` (an async fn) without `await`, add `await` or wrap in `asyncio.create_task(foo())`.
If a task was created and the program exited before it finished, await it: `await task` or `asyncio.gather(*tasks)`.
For fire-and-forget tasks, keep a strong reference: `background_tasks.add(task)` and remove on completion.
Enable debug mode: `PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1 python script.py` for richer traces.
tips: Tasks without a reference can be garbage-collected mid-flight — always store them.
`asyncio.gather` waits for everything; `asyncio.wait` lets you choose first/all.
Async code that mixes with sync (calling `time.sleep`) is its own bug.

triggers: a value is trying to be set on a copy
guides.title: Python/Pandas: SettingWithCopyWarning
steps: Identify the assignment line that triggered the warning.
Recognize the bad pattern: `df[df.x > 0]['y'] = 1` — chained indexing on a view.
Rewrite with `.loc`: `df.loc[df.x > 0, 'y'] = 1`.
If you actually wanted a separate copy, make it explicit: `df2 = df[df.x > 0].copy()`.
Re-run — the warning should disappear and the value should actually be set.
tips: Pandas can't always tell view from copy — `.loc` makes intent unambiguous.
Suppress globally only as a last resort: `pd.options.mode.chained_assignment = None`.
Pandas 3.0 plans copy-on-write — `pd.options.mode.copy_on_write = True` to preview.

guides.title: Python/numpy: shape mismatch
steps: Print the shapes of every array involved: `print(a.shape, b.shape)` before the failing line.
Recall the broadcasting rule: aligned from the right, each dim must match or be 1.
If one array is 1D where you want a column, reshape: `a.reshape(-1, 1)` or `a[:, None]`.
If you want matrix multiply, use `@` or `np.matmul`, not `*`.
If you reduced an axis somewhere upstream (e.g. `mean`), the shape collapsed — use `keepdims=True`.
Re-run; print shapes again to verify.
tips: Always print `.shape` before the failing op — most numpy bugs become obvious.
`np.newaxis` and `None` in indexing are the same thing — both add a dimension.
`einsum` makes complex shape dances explicit if broadcasting gets confusing.

guides.title: Python: SSL CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED
steps: First confirm your system clock is correct — old time breaks cert validation.
On macOS, run the bundled installer: `/Applications/Python\ 3.x/Install\ Certificates.command`.
Update certifi: `pip install --upgrade certifi`.
If behind a corporate proxy with MITM cert, point requests at the corp CA: `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE=/path/to/corp.pem`.
As a TEMPORARY test only: `requests.get(url, verify=False)` — confirms it's a cert issue.
Don't ship `verify=False` to production — fix the trust chain instead.
tips: macOS Python from python.org doesn't use the system keychain; that's why the Install Certificates step exists.
Self-signed certs need to be added to your trust store, not bypassed.
`openssl s_client -connect host:443` shows the actual cert the server presents.

guides.title: Python: memory leak in long-running script
steps: Confirm growth is real: log `psutil.Process().memory_info().rss` over time.
Snapshot allocations: `import tracemalloc; tracemalloc.start()` early, then `tracemalloc.take_snapshot().statistics('lineno')` later.
Compare two snapshots to find what grew: `snap2.compare_to(snap1, 'lineno')`.
Look for caches without bounds (dicts, lru_cache without maxsize, growing lists).
Look for closures holding references — `gc.get_referrers(obj)` shows what keeps it alive.
If C extensions are involved, use objgraph or memray for deeper analysis.
tips: `functools.lru_cache(maxsize=None)` is a classic culprit — bound it.
Global mutable state (lists, dicts) accumulates forever unless cleared.
memray gives a flamegraph of allocations — easier than tracemalloc for big apps.

guides.title: Python: slow script, find the hot spot
steps: First measure: `time python script.py` gets you a baseline.
Profile with cProfile: `python -m cProfile -o out.prof script.py`.
Inspect: `python -m pstats out.prof` then `sort cumulative` and `stats 20`.
Or visualize with snakeviz: `pip install snakeviz && snakeviz out.prof`.
For line-by-line timing on the hot function: `pip install line_profiler`, decorate with `@profile`, run `kernprof -l -v script.py`.
Optimize the actual hot spot — usually one loop, one query, or one I/O call.
tips: Don't optimize without profiling — you'll guess wrong.
`py-spy top --pid <pid>` profiles a running process without modifying it.
Often the fix is vectorization (numpy/pandas) or caching, not micro-optimization.

guides.title: Python: hanging / stuck script
steps: Hit Ctrl-C — Python prints a traceback showing exactly where it was waiting.
If Ctrl-C doesn't work (e.g. in a C extension), send SIGTERM and read the traceback.
From another terminal: `py-spy dump --pid <pid>` shows the live stack of every thread.
Common culprits: blocking I/O (no timeout), `input()` in a script, infinite loop, deadlock between threads.
Add timeouts to network calls: `requests.get(url, timeout=10)`.
If it's a deadlock, log which thread holds which lock and in what order.
tips: py-spy is the single best tool for diagnosing a frozen Python process.
Default timeouts in requests/urllib are infinite — always set one explicitly.
If your loop has no exit condition you control, you have an infinite loop.

guides.title: Python: Unicode encode/decode error
steps: Read the error: it names the codec and the byte/char that broke (e.g. 0xff).
Identify the layer: are you reading a file, decoding network bytes, or printing to a terminal?
For files: open with explicit encoding: `open(path, encoding='utf-8')`.
For bytes from network/file: `bytes.decode('utf-8', errors='replace')` to recover gracefully.
For terminal output, set `PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8`.
If the source really isn't UTF-8, identify it (often latin-1 or cp1252) and decode with that.
tips: `chardet` or `charset-normalizer` can guess the encoding of unknown bytes.
Never let Python default to your locale — be explicit with `encoding=`.
Python 3 strings are unicode; bytes are bytes. Don't mix them — decode at the edge.

guides.title: Python: psycopg2 install fails (macOS / arm)
steps: Try the prebuilt binary wheel first: `pip install psycopg2-binary` instead of `psycopg2`.
If you need the source build, install libpq: `brew install libpq` (then `brew link --force libpq`).
Ensure pg_config is on PATH: `export PATH="/opt/homebrew/opt/libpq/bin:$PATH"`.
On Apple Silicon, ensure your Python is arm64: `python -c 'import platform; print(platform.machine())'` should show `arm64`.
Retry: `pip install psycopg2`.
If still failing, consider switching to `psycopg` (v3) which has better wheels.
tips: psycopg2-binary is fine for development; psycopg2 from source is preferred in production.
If you're on x86 Python under Rosetta, brew arm64 libs won't link — match the architectures.
psycopg v3 is the modern replacement and avoids most of these install pains.

triggers: works locally fails on server python
tls works one machine not other
guides.title: Python: works on machine A, fails on machine B
steps: Compare Python versions: `python --version` on both.
Compare installed packages: `pip freeze` on both, diff them.
Compare env vars: `env | sort` — look at PATH, PYTHONPATH, SSL_CERT_FILE.
Compare OS / arch: `uname -a` — Linux glibc differences and Mac vs Linux often matter.
If it's a network call, compare connectivity (`curl -v <url>`) from each machine.
Pin everything: lock with `pip freeze > requirements.txt` then `pip install -r` on the broken machine.
tips: A reproducible env (Docker, poetry, pip-tools) eliminates 90% of these.
Different CA bundles can make TLS work on one machine and fail on another.
DNS resolution differs by network — try the IP directly to isolate.

guides.title: JS: Cannot read properties of undefined
steps: Read the error: 'Cannot read properties of undefined (reading X)'. X is the property you tried to access.
Find the access in your code: it's `something.X` where `something` is undefined.
Add a console.log right before that line: `console.log({something})` to confirm.
Trace upstream: where should `something` have been set? A function return, an API response, a prop?
Add a guard: `something?.X` (optional chaining) — fixes the crash but masks the real issue.
Fix the real cause: ensure the data is there before the read, or provide a default.
tips: Optional chaining (`?.`) is a band-aid; the real fix is understanding why it was undefined.
Async data — the component renders before the fetch resolves. Render a loading state.
Destructuring with defaults helps: `const { x = 0 } = obj ?? {}`.

guides.title: JS: X is not a function
steps: Read the error — it names what you tried to call.
console.log the value just before the call: `console.log(typeof x, x)`.
If it's undefined, the import or property access failed — check spelling and the import statement.
If it's an object, you probably forgot a method name: `x()` should be `x.doThing()`.
If it's the result of `import X from ...`, check whether the module exports default or named — your import shape may be wrong.
If it's a CommonJS/ESM mismatch, use `require('mod').default` or fix the export.
tips: `typeof` is the fastest way to know what you're dealing with.
Named vs default export is the #1 cause for new TypeScript/ESM projects.
If a library's API changed, `npm view <pkg> versions` plus changelog is your friend.

guides.title: JS: ReferenceError X is not defined
steps: Read the variable name in the error.
Check spelling and case — JS is case-sensitive.
If it's a browser global (`window`, `document`), you're running in Node — guard with `typeof window !== 'undefined'`.
If it's a Node global (`process`, `__dirname`), you're in the browser — bundle it or remove the reference.
If it's a module export, check the import line: `import { X } from '...'`.
If you forgot to declare it, add `const`, `let`, or import it.
tips: `window is not defined` during Next.js build means SSR is running browser-only code — move it inside useEffect or check `typeof`.
Strict mode catches this earlier — keep it on.
ESLint's `no-undef` would have caught most of these at edit time.

guides.title: JS: Cannot access X before initialization (TDZ)
steps: Find the line that uses X — it's running before the `let`/`const` declaration.
Move the declaration above the first use.
If it's a circular import, the binding exists but isn't initialized yet — restructure or lazy-import.
If you intended hoisting (function-scoped), use `var` or a function declaration — but prefer fixing the order.
Re-run; the error should disappear.
tips: `let` and `const` are hoisted but unusable until their declaration — that's the TDZ.
Circular imports cause TDZ when one module reads a binding from the other before it's set.
Function declarations are fully hoisted; arrow functions assigned to `const` are not.

guides.title: JS: npm install fails
steps: Read the error — look for ERESOLVE, EACCES, ETARGET, ENETUNREACH, 404.
If ERESOLVE (peer dep conflict), try `npm install --legacy-peer-deps` once to confirm — then fix versions properly.
If 404, the package name is wrong or you're hitting a private registry without auth.
If ENETUNREACH, network or proxy — try `npm config get registry` and `curl -I` to it.
Nuke and retry: `rm -rf node_modules package-lock.json && npm install`.
If still broken, try a clean Node version (`nvm install --lts && nvm use --lts`).
tips: `--legacy-peer-deps` is a workaround, not a fix — pin the offending peer correctly.
Corporate networks: `npm config set registry` to your internal mirror.
pnpm and yarn often resolve trees that npm chokes on — worth a try.

guides.title: JS: npm EACCES on global install
steps: DON'T use `sudo npm install -g` — it makes future installs worse.
Use a Node version manager that owns its prefix: install nvm or fnm.
After installing nvm: `nvm install --lts && nvm use --lts`.
Confirm: `which npm` should point inside your home dir, not `/usr/local`.
Retry the global install: `npm install -g <pkg>`.
Or, change npm's prefix to a user-owned dir: `npm config set prefix ~/.npm-global` and add `~/.npm-global/bin` to PATH.
tips: Globally installed binaries belong to your user, not root — keep it that way.
If you already ran `sudo npm` and broke perms, `sudo chown -R $(whoami) ~/.npm` fixes ownership.
Many tools (vite, eslint) work fine as project-local devDependencies — skip global install.

guides.title: JS: package-lock.json merge conflict
steps: Don't try to hand-merge a lockfile — it's machine-generated.
Accept one side (usually theirs/main): `git checkout --theirs package-lock.json`.
Delete node_modules: `rm -rf node_modules`.
Reinstall to regenerate the lockfile: `npm install`.
Stage the new lockfile: `git add package-lock.json`.
Commit the merge.
tips: Same idea applies to yarn.lock and pnpm-lock.yaml — let the tool regenerate.
Some teams ignore lockfile conflicts in PR review and just take whichever fresh install produces.
If `npm install` resolves to different versions than expected, check engines and peer deps.

triggers: cannot use import statement outside a module
guides.title: JS: ESM vs CommonJS mismatch
steps: Decide what your project is: ESM (modern, `import`) or CJS (`require`).
For ESM: add `"type": "module"` to package.json, use `.js` files with `import/export`.
For CJS: leave `"type"` out (or `"commonjs"`), use `require/module.exports`.
If you mix, name files explicitly: `.mjs` (ESM) or `.cjs` (CJS) overrides the package default.
If a dep is ESM-only and you're in CJS, dynamic import: `const x = await import('pkg')`.
Restart node — the loader caches module shape.
tips: Most modern packages are ESM-only now (chalk v5, node-fetch v3) — projects that haven't migrated hit this constantly.
TypeScript: `module: NodeNext` in tsconfig matches Node's ESM behavior.
Top-level `await` works only in ESM.

guides.title: JS/React: hydration mismatch
steps: Open the browser console — React names the differing element.
Common cause: rendering `Date.now()`, `Math.random()`, or `localStorage` directly in render — produces different output server vs client.
Move browser-only data into `useEffect` (post-mount) and store in state.
Or guard with `typeof window !== 'undefined'` and provide a stable server render.
If using user-locale formatting, render a placeholder on the server and the localized value on the client.
Check that conditional rendering doesn't depend on `window`, `document`, or user agent during initial render.
tips: Browser extensions sometimes inject DOM that React then 'mismatches' — incognito test rules that out.
Next.js `suppressHydrationWarning` silences but doesn't fix — use sparingly.
Dates and numbers are the #1 source; format them after mount.

guides.title: JS/React: invalid hook call
steps: Identify which hook is failing and where it's called.
Confirm it's called at the TOP LEVEL of a component or another hook — not inside an if/loop/callback.
Confirm the file is a component (function returning JSX), not a regular utility.
Check for duplicate React: `npm ls react` — two copies makes hooks fail.
If you're linking a local package, npm link can pull in a second React — use vite/webpack aliases to dedupe.
Restart the dev server after fixing duplicates.
tips: The three rules of hooks: only call from React functions, only at top level, same order every render.
ESLint `react-hooks/rules-of-hooks` catches most violations.
Duplicate React from `npm link` is a classic gotcha for component libraries.

triggers: each child should have unique key
guides.title: JS/React: each child should have unique key
steps: Find the `.map()` rendering a list — the JSX element returned needs a `key` prop.
Use a stable unique value: `key={item.id}`.
Only fall back to index (`key={i}`) if the list is static and items never reorder.
If items have no id, generate one when creating the item (don't generate during render — it changes on every render).
Re-run; the warning should be gone.
tips: `key={Math.random()}` is wrong — it remounts every render, killing state.
Index-as-key breaks state when items reorder or delete from the middle.
The key must be unique among SIBLINGS, not globally.

guides.title: JS/React: useEffect runs twice (StrictMode)
steps: Recognize this is intentional in dev: React.StrictMode mounts, unmounts, then remounts to catch missing cleanups.
Add a cleanup function: `return () => { /* undo the effect */ }`.
For fetches, use an AbortController and abort in cleanup.
For subscriptions, unsubscribe in cleanup.
For increments/POST calls, gate with a ref or move to a one-shot location (event handler, useEffect with proper deps).
It does NOT happen in production builds — only dev under StrictMode.
tips: Don't disable StrictMode to silence this — it's revealing a real bug.
If a fetch fires twice, your effect was missing cleanup; the dev double-fire just exposed it.
React 19's `<Activity>` and Suspense remove some of these patterns entirely.

guides.title: JS/React: state not updating / stale closure
steps: Print the value right after `setX`: it WON'T be updated — setState is async, the variable in this render is stale.
To use the new value, read it in the next render or use the functional form: `setX(prev => prev + 1)`.
If updating inside `useEffect` or `setInterval`, capture `x` via the functional setter, not the closed-over variable.
Add the missing dep to your useEffect array — ESLint exhaustive-deps catches this.
If state is an object/array, you must create a new reference: `setObj({ ...obj, k: v })`, not `obj.k = v`.
If using zustand/redux, check you're subscribing to the right slice.
tips: The functional updater `setX(prev => ...)` is immune to stale closures.
Mutating state directly is the most common 'state isn't updating' bug.
`useEffect` with `[]` deps captures initial values forever — use refs or functional updates.

guides.title: JS: unhandled promise rejection
steps: Read the rejection message — it's the underlying error.
Find the promise: it's an async call without a `.catch()` or a missed `await` inside try/catch.
Add error handling: wrap awaits in try/catch, or `.catch()` every promise chain.
For top-level promises, install a global handler: `process.on('unhandledRejection', err => ...)` in Node, or `window.addEventListener('unhandledrejection', ...)` in browser.
If a library's promise rejects silently, await its result explicitly.
In Node 15+, unhandled rejections crash the process by default — fix them at the source.
tips: Every `await` should be inside try/catch unless you're sure it can't reject.
`Promise.all` rejects on first error — use `Promise.allSettled` if you want all results.
Forgetting to await an async function is the #1 cause of phantom rejections.

guides.title: JS/Node: memory leak debug
steps: Run with inspector: `node --inspect app.js` and open chrome://inspect.
Take a heap snapshot, exercise the app to trigger the leak, take another snapshot.
Use 'Comparison' view to find objects that grew between snapshots.
Look for: event listeners never removed, closures retaining big data, growing Map/Set/array.
Patch the leak — remove listeners on cleanup, bound caches, release references.
Restart and re-snapshot to verify.
tips: `process.memoryUsage()` logs current heap to console — useful for ambient monitoring.
clinic.js doctor is a guided tool: `clinic doctor -- node app.js`.
EventEmitter without `removeListener` is the classic Node leak.

guides.title: JS/Node: out of memory
steps: First, confirm it's a real need vs a leak — see the memory-leak walkthrough if the process grows over time.
Raise the limit for legitimate cases: `node --max-old-space-size=4096 app.js` (MB).
Set globally for npm scripts via NODE_OPTIONS: `NODE_OPTIONS='--max-old-space-size=4096' npm run build`.
For builds (webpack/tsc), this is usually the right fix — they need lots of memory.
If a leak, fix it instead of raising the limit forever.
On constrained machines (CI, Docker), match the limit to container memory.
tips: Default heap is ~2GB on 64-bit Node — easy to blow past for large TS/webpack projects.
Docker: also pass memory to the container (`--memory=4g`), not just Node.
If raising the limit doesn't help, you have a real leak — go debug it.

guides.title: JS/Node: EADDRINUSE port already in use
steps: Find what's on the port: `lsof -i :3000` (mac/linux) or `netstat -ano | findstr :3000` (windows).
If it's an old run of your own app, kill it: `kill <pid>` (or `taskkill /PID <pid> /F` on windows).
Quick one-liner: `lsof -ti :3000 | xargs kill -9`.
Restart your server.
If you genuinely need two servers, change the port: `PORT=3001 npm start`.
tips: Nodemon crashes can leave the old process behind — always check what's listening.
On macOS, AirPlay Receiver squats on port 5000 — disable in System Settings.
Add a graceful shutdown (`process.on('SIGTERM', ...)`) so your dev server releases the port cleanly.

guides.title: JS/Webpack: module not found
steps: Read the error: it names the missing module and the file that imported it.
If it's an npm package, install it: `npm install <pkg>`.
If it's a local file, check the relative path — case-sensitive on Linux/CI even when it works on macOS.
Check `resolve.extensions` in webpack config if you're omitting a file extension that isn't listed.
Check `resolve.alias` for path aliases that should map (`@/` → `src/`).
Clear webpack cache: `rm -rf node_modules/.cache` and rebuild.
tips: Case mismatch is the most common cause of 'works on Mac, fails in CI'.
Aliases need to be set in BOTH webpack AND tsconfig for TS projects.
If a dep is ESM-only, you may need to mark it in `externalsType` or upgrade webpack.

guides.title: JS/Vite: HMR not working
steps: Open the browser devtools network tab — look for the WebSocket to `/__vite_hmr`. It should be open.
If blocked, check for a corporate proxy stripping WebSockets, or a service worker intercepting.
If running through Docker, expose the HMR port and set `server.hmr.host` in vite.config to the host's IP.
If working behind a tunnel (ngrok/tailscale), set `server.hmr.clientPort` to the public port.
Clear Vite cache: `rm -rf node_modules/.vite`.
Restart dev server and watch console for HMR connection messages.
tips: Service workers in dev are the #1 silent HMR killer — unregister them.
Files outside the project root won't trigger HMR unless added to `server.fs.allow`.
Some component patterns (default-export anonymous functions) break Fast Refresh — name them.

guides.title: JS/Jest: tests hang / don't exit
steps: Run with open handle detection: `jest --detectOpenHandles`.
Look at the stack — it points to the resource that's still alive (timer, server, db connection).
Close servers in afterAll: `afterAll(() => server.close())`.
Clear timers: `afterEach(() => jest.useRealTimers())` and clear any setInterval/setTimeout.
Close db pools: `afterAll(() => pool.end())`.
If you can't find it, `--forceExit` is a last resort (masks the bug, won't fix it).
tips: Any module that opens a connection on import will keep Jest alive — mock it or close it explicitly.
`testEnvironment: 'node'` for backend tests avoids jsdom overhead and weird handle leaks.
If using supertest, `app.close()` is needed even though it 'feels' synchronous.

guides.title: JS/Jest: setup file not running
steps: Confirm the setup file path in jest.config: `setupFilesAfterEach: ['<rootDir>/jest.setup.ts']`.
Distinguish `setupFiles` (runs before test framework) from `setupFilesAfterEach` (runs after framework is loaded — where `expect.extend` works).
Confirm the file actually runs by adding `console.log('SETUP')` at the top.
If running with `--config`, ensure you're pointing at the right config.
If using projects/monorepo, each project may need its own setupFiles.
Restart watch mode after config changes.
tips: `setupFilesAfterEach` is the one you want 99% of the time.
For Mocha, use `--require ./setup.js` on the CLI.
Module-level side effects in the setup file are the trick — top-level code runs once.

guides.title: JS: browser CORS error
steps: Read the exact message — it names the missing or mismatched header.
CORS is enforced by the BROWSER, not the server — curl/Postman won't reproduce it.
Fix on the SERVER: add `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: <your origin>` (or `*` for public APIs).
If preflight fails (OPTIONS), the server must respond to OPTIONS and include `Allow-Methods`, `Allow-Headers`.
If sending credentials/cookies, origin can't be `*` — must be explicit, and add `Allow-Credentials: true` plus `credentials: 'include'` on the fetch.
In dev, use the framework's proxy (Vite `server.proxy`, CRA `proxy`) to avoid CORS entirely.
tips: Disabling CORS in the browser is a hack — never ship code that needs it.
Wildcard `*` doesn't work with credentials — must list the origin explicitly.
The dev proxy is the cleanest dev-time workaround — it makes requests same-origin.

guides.title: TS: object is possibly null/undefined
steps: Read the error — TS sees a path where the value could be null/undefined.
Quick fix: use optional chaining `x?.y` to bail out if null.
If you know it's defined, narrow with an if: `if (x) { x.y }`.
If the type wrongly includes null, refine the type: `x: Foo` instead of `Foo | null`.
If from an API: validate at the boundary (zod, runtime check), then the type narrows.
Avoid `!` (non-null assertion) — it's a lie to the compiler and crashes at runtime.
tips: `strictNullChecks` is what enables this — keep it on; it catches real bugs.
User-defined type guards (`function isFoo(x): x is Foo`) narrow nicely.
Discriminated unions narrow without manual checks.

triggers: type x is not assignable to type y
guides.title: TS: type X is not assignable to type Y
steps: Read the full error — TS often points at the exact incompatible property.
Compare the two types side by side. Hover both in your editor to expand them.
If a property is missing, add it (or make it optional in the target type).
If types differ slightly (e.g. `string` vs `'a' | 'b'`), use a literal or `as const`.
If you intend the cast, use `as Y` — but understand you're overriding the checker.
If from a library type that's too strict, check if there's a generic param you can pass.
tips: TS error messages get more useful when read from the bottom up — the root cause is at the bottom.
Don't reach for `as any` reflexively — usually a tiny type fix is right there.
`satisfies` is great when you want a literal type but still type-check assignability.

guides.title: TS: exhaustiveness check on switch
steps: Define your union: `type Shape = Circle | Square | Triangle`.
Write the switch with a discriminant: `switch (shape.kind)`.
Add a `default` case that assigns to `never`: `const _: never = shape; throw new Error('Unhandled');`.
If you add a new variant later, TS errors on the never assignment until you handle it.
Use this pattern anywhere you fan out on a union — it makes refactors safe.
tips: The `never` trick converts a runtime maybe-bug into a compile-time error.
Helper: `function assertNever(x: never): never { throw ... }` for reuse.
Pair with `as const` on literal arrays for similar guarantees.

guides.title: TS: decorators not working
steps: In tsconfig.json, enable `"experimentalDecorators": true`.
If using legacy emitDecoratorMetadata (NestJS, TypeORM): also set `"emitDecoratorMetadata": true`.
Make sure your TS version matches what your framework expects (NestJS-style legacy vs TC39 standard).
If using ts-node, ensure it reads the same tsconfig (`ts-node --project tsconfig.json`).
If using SWC or esbuild, enable decorator support in their config too — they're not always on by default.
Restart your build/dev server.
tips: TS 5.0+ supports TC39 standard decorators by default — different syntax/semantics than experimental.
Frameworks like NestJS pin to experimental until they migrate.
Vite/esbuild may need `tsconfig` decorator flags AND a plugin (`@vitejs/plugin-react-swc` etc.).

triggers: could not find a declaration file
guides.title: TS: cannot find module or its type declarations
steps: Try installing community types: `npm i -D @types/<pkg>`.
If no @types exist, declare the module yourself: in `src/types/<pkg>.d.ts` add `declare module '<pkg>';`.
If types ship with the package, ensure tsconfig `moduleResolution` is `node` or `bundler` (or `nodenext`).
If the package is ESM with conditional exports, set `module` and `moduleResolution` to `nodenext`.
Check `typeRoots` and `types` in tsconfig — overly narrow values can exclude installed types.
Restart your editor's TS server after changes.
tips: VS Code: command palette → 'TypeScript: Restart TS Server' after tsconfig edits.
`moduleResolution: bundler` is the modern default for Vite/Webpack projects.
DefinitelyTyped lag is real — declaring `declare module` is a fine stopgap.

guides.title: TS: slow compile / out of memory
steps: Profile: `tsc --extendedDiagnostics --noEmit` shows where time is spent.
Enable incremental builds: `"incremental": true` in tsconfig (writes `.tsbuildinfo`).
For monorepos, switch to project references with `composite: true` and `tsc --build`.
Exclude things you don't need: `node_modules`, build output, generated files in `exclude`.
Avoid `skipLibCheck: false` unless you really need it — it slows huge projects.
If OOM: `NODE_OPTIONS='--max-old-space-size=8192' tsc`.
tips: Deeply recursive conditional types are the biggest cost — simplify when possible.
`tsc --noEmit` for type-check + a fast bundler (esbuild/swc) for transpile is a common combo.
Project references let TS skip unchanged packages.

guides.title: TS/JS: ESLint conflicts with Prettier
steps: Install: `npm i -D eslint-config-prettier`.
In your eslint config `extends`, put `'prettier'` LAST — it disables formatting rules that fight Prettier.
Remove any `eslint-plugin-prettier` integrations unless you specifically want Prettier-as-ESLint-rule (slow).
Run Prettier first, ESLint second, in your scripts.
Restart your editor's ESLint server.
tips: Let Prettier do formatting; let ESLint do logic/style rules.
Running prettier-as-ESLint-rule shows diffs as lint errors — annoying in editors. Skip it.
For monorepos, share config via a base package and extend per project.

triggers: script works in terminal but not cron
guides.title: Bash: works in terminal, not in cron
steps: Cron runs with a minimal env — no PATH, no shell aliases, no rc files.
Use absolute paths everywhere: `/usr/local/bin/python` not `python`.
Add PATH at the top of the cron entry: `PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin`.
Redirect output for debugging: `* * * * * /path/script.sh >> /tmp/script.log 2>&1`.
Check the log — cron's error is now visible.
If the script sources a file (env vars, virtualenv), source it explicitly inside the script.
tips: Cron uses /bin/sh by default, not bash — start your script with `#!/bin/bash` and run as a file.
Mail still works on some systems — `MAILTO=you@x.com` in crontab gets you the error.
On systemd machines, prefer systemd timers — better logging via `journalctl`.

guides.title: Bash: command works alone but not in `if`
steps: Remember `if` checks exit status, not command output. `if grep foo file` works; `if [ grep foo file ]` doesn't.
Use `[[ ... ]]` for bash conditionals; `[ ... ]` for POSIX.
For command-output checks: `if [[ $(cmd) == 'expected' ]]; then ...`.
Add `set -x` above the if to trace what bash actually evaluates.
Quote variables: `if [[ -z "$x" ]]; then ...` — unquoted breaks on spaces and empty strings.
Check exit code directly with `if cmd; then ...` when you only care about success.
tips: `[[` is bash-specific but much friendlier than `[`.
`set -x; ...; set +x` brackets a section to debug.
ShellCheck catches almost all of these — run it on every script.

guides.title: Bash: `if [ $X ]` doesn't behave
steps: Quote the variable: `if [ "$X" ]; then ...` — unquoted, an empty X becomes `if [ ]`.
Use `-z` for empty: `if [ -z "$X" ]`. Use `-n` for non-empty.
For numeric comparison, use `-eq -lt -gt`, not `== <`.
For string comparison, use `=` (POSIX) or `==` (inside `[[`).
Use `[[ ]]` to avoid most quoting traps.
Run with `set -x` to see expansion.
tips: Always quote variables in `[ ]` — it's the #1 source of test bugs.
`[[ ]]` doesn't word-split — safer for variables and easier to read.
ShellCheck flags every one of these mistakes.

guides.title: Bash: variable not visible after subshell
steps: Common cause: piping into `while` creates a subshell — vars set inside don't survive.
Replace `cmd | while read line; do X=...; done` with `while read line; do X=...; done < <(cmd)`.
Or use a here-string: `while read line; do ...; done <<< "$output"`.
Avoid `()` — that's a subshell. Use `{ }` for grouping in the same shell.
`export` makes a variable visible to children — not back to parent.
Verify by echoing after the loop.
tips: Process substitution `< <(cmd)` is the cleanest fix for the pipe-into-while trap.
Bash has lastpipe option: `shopt -s lastpipe` keeps the last segment of a pipe in the current shell.
POSIX sh doesn't have process substitution — `while read` from a temp file as a fallback.

guides.title: Bash: script exits silently / set -e gotchas
steps: Start every script with `set -euo pipefail` to fail fast and surface bugs.
Know the gotchas: `set -e` does NOT trigger in `if`, `&&/||`, `!`, or `()` contexts — by design.
If you `cmd | other`, only the LAST command's status matters unless `set -o pipefail`.
Trap errors for debugging: `trap 'echo "line $LINENO failed"' ERR`.
Add `set -x` to trace every command — verbose but tells you where it died.
Check status explicitly after risky commands: `cmd || { echo fail; exit 1; }`.
tips: `pipefail` is what most people miss — without it, `false | true` succeeds.
`set -u` catches typos in variable names (`$wrong_name` → error).
ShellCheck on every script — it pays for itself in an afternoon.

triggers: works locally fails in ci bash
guides.title: Bash: works locally, fails in CI
steps: Echo PATH in CI: `echo "$PATH"` — compare with your local `echo $PATH`.
Use absolute paths in scripts: `/usr/bin/git` not `git`.
Pin tool versions in CI (Node, Python, etc.) instead of trusting the runner default.
If a tool was installed by a previous step, ensure that step ran on the same runner/job (caching matters).
Reproduce locally with the same Docker image CI uses: `docker run -it <ci-image>`.
Add `set -x` to CI script to see what runs.
tips: GitHub Actions Ubuntu image is NOT a fresh Ubuntu — many tools preinstalled. Don't assume the same elsewhere.
CI workers are ephemeral — anything installed in one job is gone in the next unless explicitly cached.
Use `actions/setup-node` etc. for reproducible tool versions.

guides.title: Bash: permission denied (even with sudo)
steps: Check the file has execute bit: `ls -l file.sh`. If no `x`, add it: `chmod +x file.sh`.
Check ownership: `ls -l file.sh` — `chown $USER file.sh` if owned by root.
If sudo also fails, the filesystem may be mounted noexec — check `mount | grep <path>`.
On macOS, files quarantined from downloads: `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine file.sh`.
If a script's shebang points to a missing interpreter, you get permission-like errors — verify with `file script.sh`.
Check parent directory perms — even with file +x, you need +x on every ancestor dir.
tips: `./script.sh` requires +x; `bash script.sh` only requires +r — useful for diagnosis.
macOS Gatekeeper blocks unsigned downloads even with +x — `xattr -d` clears it.
/tmp is sometimes noexec on hardened systems — copy to a writeable, executable dir.

guides.title: Bash: quoted argument with spaces breaks
steps: Always quote variables that may contain spaces: `cp "$src" "$dst"`.
When passing a path to a command, quote it at the point of use, not just on assignment.
When iterating files, use globs not `ls`: `for f in *.txt; do echo "$f"; done`.
For arrays of args, use bash arrays: `args=(--foo "my value") && cmd "${args[@]}"`.
For arguments built up over time, use `"${arr[@]}"` not `"$arr"`.
Run `set -x` to see exactly how bash splits your command.
tips: `"$@"` preserves args with spaces; `$*` collapses them.
ShellCheck warns on every unquoted variable — listen to it.
Avoid eval-on-strings; use arrays for command construction.

guides.title: Bash: heredoc variable expansion
steps: Default heredoc expands variables: `cat <<EOF` — `$var` becomes its value.
To prevent expansion, quote the marker: `cat <<'EOF'` — content is literal.
To preserve indentation, use `<<-EOF` (strips leading TABS only, not spaces).
If embedding into another tool (e.g. ssh), think carefully about which shell expands — the local or remote.
Use `printf '%s\n' "$value"` instead of heredoc if you only need one variable substituted.
Test with `cat <<EOF` first to see exactly what your shell produces.
tips: Quoting the EOF is the on/off switch for variable expansion.
ssh: outer shell expands first; whatever you send is the literal command on the other end.
Indented heredocs need TABS, not spaces — `<<-` strips tabs only.

guides.title: Bash: source vs ./ confusion
steps: `./script.sh` runs in a child shell — its vars and cd don't affect you.
`source script.sh` (or `. script.sh`) runs in your current shell — vars persist.
If you want a script to set env vars for your shell, you must source it.
If you want isolation (clean exit, no side effects), execute it.
Activation scripts (`source .venv/bin/activate`) MUST be sourced — that's how they work.
Add a self-check inside the script: `(return 0 2>/dev/null) || { echo 'must be sourced'; exit 1; }`.
tips: If you find yourself wishing exec changed env, you want source.
Sourcing also means a `set -e` in the script affects YOUR shell — be aware.
Function definitions only stick around if you source the file that defines them.

guides.title: Bash: PATH ordering issue
steps: List all candidates: `which -a <command>` (or `type -a <command>` in bash).
Inspect PATH: `echo "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n'`.
The first directory containing the binary wins. Reorder PATH if needed.
Add to front: `export PATH="/desired/dir:$PATH"`.
Use `hash -r` to flush bash's cache after PATH changes.
Persist the change in your shell rc (`.bashrc`, `.zshrc`).
tips: Homebrew often puts its prefix near the front; on Apple Silicon that's `/opt/homebrew/bin`.
Tools like nvm/pyenv install shims that need to be in PATH BEFORE the system binaries.
`command -v <name>` is more portable than `which`.

guides.title: Bash: locale / encoding issues
steps: Print current locale: `locale`. Look for entries set to `POSIX` or empty.
Set sane defaults in your shell rc: `export LANG=en_US.UTF-8 LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8`.
On Linux, generate locales if missing: `sudo locale-gen en_US.UTF-8`.
On macOS, default Terminal.app sets LANG by default; iTerm may not — set explicitly.
For sort, awk, sed differences, override per command: `LC_ALL=C sort file` for byte-order sort.
Restart your shell after rc changes.
tips: `LC_ALL=C` makes everything byte-wise — fast and predictable, but ASCII-only.
SSH on a server: locale isn't always forwarded — set on the server side.
Docker images: many minimal images lack locales — install `locales` or use the C locale.

guides.title: Bash: ssh hangs on connect
steps: Verbose: `ssh -vvv user@host` — shows exactly where it stalls.
If stuck on 'expecting SSH_MSG_KEX_ECDH_REPLY', it's often MTU/firewall — try `ssh -o IPQoS=throughput user@host`.
If DNS slow, try the IP directly to confirm: `ssh user@<ip>`.
Disable GSSAPI auth (a common stall): `-o GSSAPIAuthentication=no`.
If hanging on banner, server is overloaded or fail2ban is throttling you.
Set KeepAlive for unreliable links: `-o ServerAliveInterval=30`.
tips: Add stable settings to `~/.ssh/config` per-host once you find what works.
`UseRoaming no` was a 2016 fix and is no longer relevant — don't add it.
`mosh` survives flaky networks better than ssh.

triggers: ssh works interactively fails in script
guides.title: Bash: ssh works locally, fails in script
steps: If you see 'Pseudo-terminal will not be allocated', use `-t` to force TTY or `-T` to suppress.
If commands run remotely need a TTY (sudo with password, vim), force with `-t`.
If using agent forwarding (`-A`), confirm `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` is set in the script env.
Cron/CI: no agent, no terminal — use a key with no passphrase or use a deploy token.
Confirm host key trust: in scripts, pre-populate `~/.ssh/known_hosts` instead of disabling StrictHostKeyChecking.
Run the script with `set -x` to see exact ssh invocation.
tips: Don't pipe a password into ssh — use keys. If you must, `sshpass` exists but is fragile.
`ssh -o BatchMode=yes` makes ssh fail fast in scripts instead of prompting.
GitHub Actions ssh agent: use `webfactory/ssh-agent` action to set up properly.

guides.title: Bash: rsync trailing slash gotcha
steps: Recall the rule: `rsync src/` copies the CONTENTS of src; `rsync src` copies src ITSELF (as a subdir).
If you got a nested src/src/, you forgot the trailing slash on source.
If you got loose files where you wanted a folder, you added a trailing slash you didn't want.
Destination trailing slash doesn't matter — only the source.
Always dry-run first: `rsync -avn src/ dest/` (the `n` is dry-run).
Confirm the diff with `--itemize-changes` for verbose per-file info.
tips: Trailing-slash semantics: src/ means 'this folder's contents', src means 'this folder'.
`--delete` mirrors — make sure your dry-run shows what you expect before removing it.
`-a` is the workhorse flag — archive (recursive, perms, links, times).

guides.title: Git: resolve a merge conflict
steps: Find conflicted files: `git status` lists them under 'Unmerged paths'.
Open each file. Look for the markers: `<<<<<<<` (yours), `=======` (separator), `>>>>>>>` (theirs).
Edit the file: pick one side, blend both, or rewrite. Delete every line containing a marker.
Save the file.
Stage the resolved file: `git add <filename>`.
Repeat for each conflicted file.
Finish the merge: `git commit` (Git provides a default message — no -m needed).
Verify: `git status` should show 'working tree clean'.
tips: Panic button: `git merge --abort` rolls back to before the merge.
VS Code / IntelliJ show conflicts with 'Accept Current / Incoming / Both' buttons in the gutter.
Inspect the three sides before deciding: `git log --merge -p <file>` shows commits involved.

guides.title: Git: detached HEAD — what it means and how to recover
steps: Recognize the state: `git status` says 'HEAD detached at <commit>' — you're on a commit, not a branch.
If you DID make commits and want to keep them: create a branch here: `git switch -c my-fix`.
If you DIDN'T make commits: just switch back: `git switch main` (or wherever).
If you made commits and already left, find them: `git reflog` shows recent HEAD positions.
Recover with: `git switch -c rescue <commit-from-reflog>`.
Confirm: `git log --oneline -5` shows your work.
tips: Detached HEAD isn't dangerous — it's just 'no branch points here'. Branch before committing.
`git switch -` jumps back to the previous branch (like `cd -`).
reflog keeps moves for ~90 days by default — plenty of time to rescue.

triggers: git pushed to main by mistake
guides.title: Git: pushed to the wrong branch
steps: First decide: do you need to remove the commits from the wrong branch, or is moving them enough?
Move commits to the right branch: `git switch correct-branch && git cherry-pick <bad-commit>...<HEAD-of-wrong>`.
Push to the right branch: `git push origin correct-branch`.
Now remove from wrong branch: `git switch wrong-branch && git reset --hard <commit-before-bad>`.
Force-push the wrong branch BACK: `git push --force-with-lease origin wrong-branch`.
Tell collaborators — anyone who pulled needs to reset their local copy.
tips: `--force-with-lease` is safer than `--force` — fails if someone else pushed in between.
Never force-push to `main` on a shared repo without coordination.
GitHub's branch protection can prevent these mistakes — enable it.

guides.title: Git: committed to wrong branch (not pushed yet)
steps: Note the commit you want to move: `git log --oneline -5`.
Create or switch to the right branch from where you are: `git branch correct-branch`.
Reset the wrong branch back: `git reset --hard HEAD~1` (or further back if multiple commits).
Switch: `git switch correct-branch` — your commits are here now.
Confirm with `git log` on both branches.
Push the correct branch.
tips: If you haven't pushed yet, this is fully safe — no one else is affected.
`git branch <name>` creates without switching; pair with reset on the old branch.
If the wrong branch shared other commits, only `reset` back as far as the misplaced ones.

guides.title: Git: lost commits — find with reflog
steps: Run `git reflog` — every HEAD movement in the last ~90 days is here.
Find the SHA that was your last good state.
Inspect it: `git show <sha>` or `git log <sha> -5`.
Recover by branching from it: `git branch rescue <sha>` then `git switch rescue`.
Or hard reset your current branch back to it: `git reset --hard <sha>` (destructive — be sure first).
Push the rescued branch.
tips: reflog is your local-only safety net — it survives most accidents.
Deleted branches still appear in reflog by their last position.
If reflog doesn't have it, `git fsck --lost-found` looks at dangling objects.

guides.title: Git: accidentally `git reset --hard`
steps: Don't make more commits — that's the only thing that can really lose your work.
Run `git reflog` — find the SHA from BEFORE the reset.
Reset back: `git reset --hard <good-sha>`.
Verify with `git log --oneline -5`.
If uncommitted changes were lost (not just commits): `git fsck --lost-found` may turn up dangling blobs.
Going forward, prefer `git switch -c <name>` before risky operations.
tips: Commits live ~90 days in the local reflog even after reset — you have time.
Uncommitted, unstaged changes are NOT recoverable — they were never in git.
`git stash` before destructive operations as a habit.

guides.title: Git: accidentally committed a secret
steps: ROTATE the secret immediately — assume it's compromised even if you remove it.
Add it to .gitignore so it doesn't return.
Remove from the latest commit only: `git rm --cached <file> && git commit --amend`.
If already pushed and the secret is in older commits, you must rewrite history: use `git-filter-repo --invert-paths --path <file>` (or BFG Repo-Cleaner).
Force-push the rewritten history: `git push --force-with-lease`.
Tell collaborators to re-clone — their old clones still have the secret.
tips: Rotation is the only real fix; history rewrites don't help once it's been seen.
GitHub's secret-scanning alerts catch many common token formats automatically.
Use pre-commit hooks (`detect-secrets`, `gitleaks`) to catch them before they're committed.

guides.title: Git: force-push went wrong on a shared branch
steps: Don't panic — anyone who pulled before the force-push still has the old commits locally.
Ask each teammate: `git reflog` on their machine for the pre-pull HEAD.
On their machine: `git push <remote> <good-sha>:refs/heads/<branch>` recovers the remote.
Or: `git push --force-with-lease <remote> <local-branch>:<branch>` from a teammate who still has good state.
After recovery, communicate to whoever made the bad push.
Set up branch protection to prevent recurrence.
tips: GitHub's branch protection / 'do not allow force pushes' prevents this entirely — turn it on.
`--force-with-lease` is much safer than `--force`. Make it your default alias.
Reflog on the originator's machine is also valuable — check there too.

guides.title: Git: stuck mid-rebase
steps: Check state: `git status` — it tells you what's pending and offers commands.
If you want out: `git rebase --abort` returns you to the pre-rebase state.
If you've made progress and want to continue: resolve conflicts, `git add` resolved files, `git rebase --continue`.
If you want to skip a problematic commit: `git rebase --skip`.
If you've forgotten what you were rebasing onto: `cat .git/rebase-merge/onto` or check reflog.
After finishing, verify with `git log --oneline`.
tips: `git rebase --abort` is ALWAYS safe — it returns you to where you started.
Interactive rebase (`-i`) keeps a TODO list at `.git/rebase-merge/git-rebase-todo`.
If terrified, `git switch -c backup` before starting any rebase.

guides.title: Git: cannot push, non-fast-forward
steps: The remote has commits you don't. You need to integrate them first.
Fetch latest: `git fetch origin`.
Choose: merge (`git merge origin/<branch>`) or rebase (`git rebase origin/<branch>`).
Resolve any conflicts that arise.
Push: `git push`.
If you intentionally want to overwrite the remote, force-push: `git push --force-with-lease` (only for branches you own).
tips: Set rebase as default for pulls: `git config --global pull.rebase true`.
Never force-push to shared branches without coordination.
`git pull` does fetch + merge in one go if you prefer.

triggers: your local changes would be overwritten
guides.title: Git: cannot pull — local changes would be overwritten
steps: Decide whether to keep your local edits or discard them.
To keep them: `git stash`, then `git pull`, then `git stash pop`.
To discard: `git checkout -- <files>` or `git restore <files>`.
If you want to commit before pulling: `git add -A && git commit -m 'wip'` then `git pull --rebase`.
If the stash pop conflicts, you'll get conflict markers — resolve like a merge.
Verify with `git status`.
tips: Stash is the safest 'hold this for a sec' move.
`git stash --include-untracked` if you also have new files.
After `stash pop`, your stash entry is dropped on success — keep it with `stash apply`.

guides.title: Git: stash pop conflict
steps: Recognize: `git stash pop` triggered a conflict — your stash is still saved.
Resolve like a normal merge conflict: open files, fix markers, save.
Stage the resolved files: `git add <files>`.
DO NOT run `git commit` — you're not in a merge state. The conflict is just informational.
Drop the stash if you no longer need it: `git stash drop`.
Confirm with `git status`.
tips: Conflicted pop leaves the stash in place (unlike a clean pop) — `stash list` shows it.
Use `git stash apply` instead of `pop` if you want the stash kept around regardless.
If totally lost, `git checkout --theirs/--ours <file>` picks a side.

triggers: git status shows changes I didn't make
guides.title: Git: files show as changed but I didn't change them
steps: Run `git diff <file>` to see WHAT git thinks changed.
If the whole file 'changed' with no visible diff, it's line endings (CRLF vs LF).
Set the right endings: `git config core.autocrlf true` (Windows) or `false` (Mac/Linux).
Add a `.gitattributes` file to make endings explicit per file type.
Renormalize: `git add --renormalize .` and commit.
For file-mode (+x) changes: `git config core.filemode false` on Windows/WSL boundaries.
tips: .gitattributes is the durable fix — config alone varies by clone.
`git diff --stat` shows which files have content vs metadata changes.
`git diff -w` ignores whitespace if you want to confirm content is identical.

guides.title: Git: submodule out of sync
steps: Check what's wrong: `git status` — submodule may show 'modified' or 'new commits'.
Sync to the recorded commit: `git submodule update --init --recursive`.
If you want the submodule's latest: `git submodule update --remote`.
If the URL changed: `git submodule sync --recursive` then update.
If totally broken, deinit and re-init: `git submodule deinit -f <path>` then `git submodule update --init <path>`.
Commit any submodule SHA changes you intend in the parent repo.
tips: Submodules track a SHA, not a branch — `--remote` checks out the branch tip.
`git clone --recurse-submodules` pulls submodules at clone time.
Many teams replace submodules with monorepo tools (git-subtree, npm workspaces) to avoid this pain.

guides.title: Git: large file rejected by GitHub (>100MB)
steps: Decide: do you actually need this file in git? Consider artifacts/CDN if not.
If yes, set up Git LFS: `git lfs install` then `git lfs track '*.psd'` (per filetype).
Commit the .gitattributes file.
Re-add the file: `git add <file>` — LFS will handle it.
If already in history, you must rewrite to remove it: use `git-filter-repo --strip-blobs-bigger-than 100M`.
Force-push and re-add via LFS.
tips: GitHub Pro plans include LFS quota; free has a small allowance.
Once big files are in git history, they live there forever unless you rewrite.
Common offenders: built binaries, node_modules, generated assets — add to .gitignore.

guides.title: Git: authentication failed
steps: Determine remote protocol: `git remote -v` — HTTPS or SSH.
For HTTPS to GitHub: passwords don't work anymore. Use a personal access token in place of password.
Or switch to SSH: `git remote set-url origin git@github.com:user/repo.git`.
Test SSH: `ssh -T git@github.com` — should greet you by username.
For HTTPS, set up the credential helper: `git config --global credential.helper osxkeychain` (mac), `manager` (windows), `cache` or `store` (linux).
Retry the push.
tips: GitHub deprecated password auth — token or SSH is your only option.
GitHub CLI (`gh auth login`) sets up credentials cleanly.
Multiple accounts: use `~/.ssh/config` Host aliases to pick the right key per repo.

guides.title: Git: GitHub Pages not updating after push
steps: Check the Actions tab — Pages now deploys via a workflow. Look for build errors.
Confirm Pages is enabled and points at the correct branch (Settings → Pages).
Wait 1-5 minutes — propagation isn't instant.
Force a browser cache bypass: hard reload (Cmd+Shift+R) or open in incognito.
Check the live URL with curl: `curl -I https://user.github.io/repo/` — Last-Modified shows when it actually deployed.
If using a custom domain, confirm DNS and that 'Enforce HTTPS' is checked.
tips: CDN cache can hold for ~10 minutes — incognito bypasses it.
Jekyll builds happen on GitHub side — check the build log in Actions.
404s on direct routes are usually a missing 404.html for SPAs.

guides.title: Git: branch is ahead/behind — what to do
steps: Read the status: 'ahead by N' = you have commits remote doesn't. 'behind by N' = remote has commits you don't.
'Diverged' = both have commits the other doesn't — you must merge or rebase.
If just ahead: `git push`.
If just behind: `git pull`.
If diverged: `git pull --rebase` (clean linear history) or `git pull` (merge commit).
After: confirm `git status` says 'up to date'.
tips: `git status` numbers are based on the last `git fetch` — run fetch for an up-to-date view.
Set `pull.rebase = true` for cleaner history by default.
`git log --oneline --graph --all` visualizes divergence beautifully.

guides.title: Git: cherry-pick conflict
steps: `git status` shows which files conflicted.
Resolve like a merge — edit files, remove `<<<` markers.
Stage the resolved files: `git add <files>`.
Continue: `git cherry-pick --continue`.
To bail out completely: `git cherry-pick --abort`.
To skip the problematic commit (when cherry-picking a range): `git cherry-pick --skip`.
tips: Cherry-pick is for moving an isolated commit. For ranges, consider rebase-onto.
If the same commit is already partially applied, `--strategy=recursive -X theirs` can resolve simple cases.
`git cherry-pick -x <sha>` adds a 'cherry-picked from' note in the message.

guides.title: Git: rebase vs merge for pulling
steps: Default `git pull` = fetch + merge. Creates a merge commit if histories diverged.
`git pull --rebase` = fetch + replay your commits ON TOP of remote — linear history, no merge commit.
Pick rebase for personal branches and clean history. Pick merge to preserve context of parallel work.
Pick a default and stick to it: `git config --global pull.rebase true` for rebase by default.
Never rebase commits that other people are working on — only your own untyped feature branches.
For PR branches into main: usually rebase; for long-lived branches: usually merge.
tips: Linear history is easier to bisect; merge commits preserve actual time-order.
GitHub's 'Squash and merge' is the most common compromise.
`pull.ff = only` rejects pulls that aren't fast-forward — forces you to pick consciously.

guides.title: Git: undo the last commit
steps: Decide: keep the changes (in working tree) or throw them away?
Keep changes (most common): `git reset --soft HEAD~1` — un-commits but leaves changes staged.
Or `git reset HEAD~1` (mixed, the default) — un-commits and unstages, files remain edited.
Throw away entirely: `git reset --hard HEAD~1` — DESTRUCTIVE, gone.
If already pushed: `git revert HEAD` creates a NEW commit that undoes the bad one — safe on shared branches.
Verify with `git log --oneline -5`.
tips: `reset` rewrites history; `revert` adds new history. Use revert for shared branches.
`--soft` is the least scary — your work is preserved and staged for re-commit.
If you reset --hard by accident, reflog rescues you.

guides.title: Network: server unreachable / connection refused
steps: Resolve DNS: `dig <host>` or `nslookup <host>` — does the name return an IP?
Ping the IP: `ping <ip>` — confirms basic reachability (some servers block ping, that's fine).
Check port: `nc -zv <host> <port>` or `telnet <host> <port>` — does TCP connect?
If TCP fails: firewall, service not running, or wrong port.
If TCP works but HTTPS fails: TLS issue — `openssl s_client -connect host:443`.
Curl with verbose: `curl -v https://host/path` — see every step.
tips: 'Connection refused' = nothing's listening. 'Timeout' = packets aren't getting there.
Test from a different network (phone hotspot) to isolate local issues.
`mtr <host>` is traceroute + ping combined — great for intermittent connectivity.

guides.title: Network: DNS not resolving
steps: Try a public resolver to isolate: `dig @8.8.8.8 <host>`.
If that works, your local DNS is the issue — check `/etc/resolv.conf` or system DNS settings.
Flush local DNS cache: `sudo dscacheutil -flushcache` (mac), `ipconfig /flushdns` (windows), `sudo systemd-resolve --flush-caches` (linux).
Check `/etc/hosts` for a stale override: `cat /etc/hosts`.
If on a VPN, your DNS may be routed through it — test with VPN off.
If a new domain, give DNS propagation up to 48 hours.
tips: `dig +trace <host>` walks the resolution from the root down — pinpoints where it breaks.
DNS over HTTPS in browsers can mask /etc/hosts changes — test with curl.
Corporate networks often filter DNS — try the company's documented resolver.

guides.title: Network: TLS / certificate error
steps: Inspect the cert: `openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host </dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -text`.
Check expiry: dates in the output.
Check the chain: `openssl s_client -showcerts` lists every cert sent.
Verify SNI: `-servername` matches what the server expects.
If self-signed, add to system trust or use `--insecure` for testing only.
Confirm system clock is accurate — wrong time invalidates many certs.
tips: SSL Labs (ssllabs.com/ssltest) gives a full diagnostic for public-facing endpoints.
Let's Encrypt certs renew every 90 days — a forgotten renewal is the most common cause of sudden TLS errors.
Intermediate certs missing from the chain is a common server-side bug — `--showcerts` reveals it.

guides.title: Perf: website is slow
steps: Open Chrome DevTools → Network: hard reload and look at the waterfall. What's the long bar?
If TTFB is long, server-side is slow — profile backend, not frontend.
If many small requests, consolidate or add HTTP/2.
If large bundles, check Coverage tab for unused JS/CSS; tree-shake or code-split.
Open DevTools → Lighthouse and run an audit — it ranks the biggest wins.
Open DevTools → Performance, record a load, look at the long-tasks in Main thread.
tips: TTFB > 500ms is a backend problem; large LCP image is a frontend problem.
WebPageTest (webpagetest.org) gives a third-party view from many locations.
Lazy-load below-the-fold images: ``.

guides.title: API: 401 but token looks right
steps: Confirm the header is being sent: curl with `-v` and check Authorization line.
Confirm the exact format: `Authorization: Bearer <token>` — case, space, no quotes.
Check token expiration — JWTs often expire in minutes; refresh if so.
Confirm you're hitting the right environment (dev/staging/prod tokens don't cross).
Try the token in Postman/curl directly — if it works there, your code is mangling the header.
Check token scopes — the call may need a scope your token lacks.
tips: JWT.io decodes a JWT in the browser — check `exp` claim.
Some APIs use `Token <x>` or `ApiKey <x>` — confirm the exact scheme in their docs.
Trailing whitespace in env vars is a classic 401 cause.

guides.title: API: 403 forbidden
steps: Confirm 401 vs 403: 401 = bad auth, 403 = good auth, no permission.
Check user/role permissions on the resource — does this account own/access it?
Check scopes on the token — many tokens are limited.
Check IP allowlist — some APIs restrict by source IP.
Some APIs return 403 instead of 404 for resources you can't see — confirm the resource exists with a higher-privilege account.
Check rate-limit headers — some services return 403 for soft bans.
tips: If switching from staging to prod credentials gives 403, the resource may exist only in one env.
AWS S3 returns 403 for both 'no access' and 'no such key' if listing is denied — confusing.
Server-side, log the exact reason in your 403 responses — saves clients hours.

guides.title: API: 429 too many requests
steps: Read response headers — `Retry-After`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, `X-RateLimit-Reset` tell you the limit.
Implement client-side retry with backoff: respect `Retry-After`, exponential delay otherwise.
Batch requests where the API supports it.
Cache responses — don't re-fetch unchanged data.
If you legitimately need more, request a higher tier or use multiple API keys (only if allowed).
Add jitter to retries: random delay to avoid thundering-herd.
tips: Exponential backoff with jitter is the standard pattern — every cloud SDK does it.
If parallel requests cause 429s, add a concurrency limit (p-limit, semaphore).
Stop ASAP on 429 — repeated hits can extend the ban.

guides.title: API: 500 internal server error
steps: First confirm: is it always 500, or intermittent? Retry to find out.
Check the response body — many APIs include diagnostic info.
If you control the server: check logs around the time of the failure.
Reproduce with the smallest possible request — strip headers and body until it works, then add back.
Check upstream dependencies — DB, cache, downstream APIs.
If it's a third-party API, check their status page.
tips: 500 is the server's fault; 4xx is the client's. Confirm before assuming.
If logs aren't accessible, request IDs in the response let you correlate with backend logs later.
Sentry/Datadog on the server side gives stack traces for 500s — invaluable.

guides.title: Docker: build fails
steps: Read the error — Docker shows which step (RUN/COPY/ETC) and the underlying command's output.
Reproduce just the bad step by running an interactive container at the previous stage: `docker run -it <previous-stage-image> sh`.
If a RUN command fails, run it manually inside the container to debug.
Check .dockerignore — needed files may be excluded.
Check FROM image — pinned versions disappear sometimes; use a specific digest.
Try `--no-cache` to rule out stale layers.
tips: BuildKit gives much better error output — use `DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1`.
Multi-stage builds: the last stage matters — earlier stages may succeed/fail silently.
`docker buildx build --progress=plain` shows full logs for every step.

guides.title: Docker: container exits immediately
steps: Check exit code: `docker ps -a` shows STATUS like 'Exited (1) 5 seconds ago'.
Read logs: `docker logs <container>` — usually has the error.
If exit code 0, the entrypoint completed normally — your CMD is a one-shot, not a server.
If non-zero, the process crashed. Run interactively to debug: `docker run -it --entrypoint sh <image>`.
Verify your CMD/ENTRYPOINT actually starts a foreground process — backgrounded processes exit the container.
For dev, override with `docker run -it <image> sh` to poke around.
tips: Containers run as long as PID 1 runs. `nohup app &` exits because PID 1 died.
Don't `init` daemons inside containers — let the orchestrator handle restarts.
`tail -f /dev/null` is a debugging trick to keep a misconfigured container alive.

guides.title: Docker: container can't reach host service
steps: Inside the container, `localhost` means the container itself — not your host.
On Mac/Windows Docker Desktop: use `host.docker.internal` to reach the host.
On Linux: add `--add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway` to `docker run`.
Alternatively run with `--network host` (Linux only) to share the host's network namespace.
Confirm the host service is bound to all interfaces (0.0.0.0), not just 127.0.0.1.
Test from inside: `docker exec -it <c> curl host.docker.internal:<port>`.
tips: Linux Docker doesn't have host.docker.internal by default — add it explicitly.
Services bound to 127.0.0.1 on the host aren't reachable from containers — bind to 0.0.0.0.
On Docker Compose, services see each other by service name — no host.docker.internal needed.

guides.title: Docker: port not exposed
steps: Run with `-p <hostPort>:<containerPort>`: e.g. `docker run -p 8080:80 nginx`.
Verify with `docker port <container>` — lists actual mappings.
Inside the container, confirm the service is listening on the container port and on 0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1.
From the host, try `curl localhost:<hostPort>`.
EXPOSE in a Dockerfile is informational; you still need `-p` (or `-P` for all exposed).
Firewall on host can block — check ufw/iptables/Windows Firewall.
tips: Common mistake: app listens on 127.0.0.1 inside the container — invisible from outside.
docker-compose: `ports:` is the equivalent of `-p`.
`docker run -P` (uppercase) maps every EXPOSEd port to a random host port.

guides.title: Docker: image too large
steps: Inspect layer sizes: `docker history <image>` or `dive <image>`.
Switch base to slim/alpine: `python:3.11-slim` vs `python:3.11`.
Use multi-stage builds: build in a fat stage, copy artifacts into a slim final stage.
Combine RUN steps to reduce layers: `RUN apt-get update && apt-get install ... && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*`.
Exclude dev deps from prod images.
Add a comprehensive .dockerignore (node_modules, .git, tests, docs).
tips: Alpine is small but uses musl libc — some Python wheels break. Use slim if so.
`dive` is the best image-explorer; it shows wasted space per layer.
Distroless images (Google) give the smallest secure final images.

guides.title: K8s: pod in CrashLoopBackOff
steps: Read logs of the LAST run: `kubectl logs <pod>` shows current; `kubectl logs <pod> --previous` shows prior crash.
Describe the pod: `kubectl describe pod <pod>` — events at the bottom often explain.
Check resource limits — OOMKilled shows up here.
Run the image locally to reproduce: `docker run -it <image>`.
Check liveness probe — too aggressive can cause loops.
If env or configmaps are wrong, fix and roll the deployment: `kubectl rollout restart deployment <name>`.
tips: `kubectl logs --previous` is the magic flag — most diagnoses live there.
OOMKilled means the limit is too low or the app leaks — bump or fix.
Backoff delays double up to 5min — fix fast or it gets slow to verify.

guides.title: K8s: pod in ImagePullBackOff
steps: `kubectl describe pod <pod>` — events section names the registry error.
Common: bad image name/tag. Verify with `docker pull <image>` from your machine.
If private registry: ensure an imagePullSecret is configured and referenced in the pod spec.
Create the secret: `kubectl create secret docker-registry <name> --docker-server=... --docker-username=... --docker-password=...`.
Reference in the pod: `imagePullSecrets: [name: <name>]`.
For ECR/GCR/ACR, use the cloud-provider auth helpers.
tips: Tags can move; pinning to a digest (`sha256:...`) is most reliable.
Network policies can block egress to image registries — check those too.
DockerHub rate limits hit hard — authenticated pulls have a higher quota.

triggers: github actions only fails in ci
guides.title: CI: step fails only in CI
steps: Diff env: print `env | sort` in CI vs locally. Common diffs: PATH, NODE_VERSION, language locale.
Match versions: pin Node/Python/etc. in CI to match local exactly.
Run the same Docker image CI uses, locally: `docker run -it <image>`.
Add `set -x` (bash) or equivalent to see exact commands.
Check for hidden state: CI machines are fresh; if you assume a tool is installed, install it.
Re-run with debug logging: set `ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG=true` in repo secrets for GitHub Actions.
tips: GitHub Actions: `act` can run workflows locally — closer to CI than your own shell.
File case-sensitivity bites: Linux is strict, macOS isn't by default.
If a test relies on time/locale, set TZ and LANG explicitly in CI.

guides.title: CI: GitHub Actions can't access a secret
steps: Confirm the secret is set: Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions. Check name/case.
Reference correctly: `${{ secrets.MY_SECRET }}` — case matters, no spaces.
Secrets are NOT available to PRs from forks for security — workflows triggered by fork PRs see them as empty.
Secrets aren't available in `pull_request_target` outside the default branch's workflow file — use carefully.
Env scope: `env:` at job vs step level matters.
Log a masked check: `echo "len=${#MY_SECRET}"` to see if it's populated.
tips: GitHub auto-masks secrets in logs — but echo'ing them still leaks via Base64 etc. Don't try to print them.
Environment secrets (under 'Environments') allow per-env scoping.
Organization secrets cover many repos at once.

guides.title: CI: test passes locally, fails in CI
steps: Run the SAME container/image CI uses, locally.
Match Node/Python/etc. versions exactly.
Check for ordering dependence: `--randomize` or shuffle tests.
Check for time/timezone assumptions — CI is usually UTC.
Check for filesystem case sensitivity — CI Linux is strict.
Check for parallel-test interference: shared DB, ports, files.
