tips: Test pollution: one test leaves state another depends on — shuffling reveals this.
Fixed seeds for randomness aren't 'fixed' across runtimes — verify on CI's runtime.
Snapshots can differ by line endings — `.gitattributes` to enforce LF.

guides.title: CI: build works locally, fails in CI
steps: Match runtime versions: pin Node/Python/etc. in CI config to what you use locally.
Clean install locally to compare: `rm -rf node_modules && npm ci`.
Use `npm ci` (not `install`) in CI to honor the lockfile exactly.
Check for case-sensitivity in imports — Linux is strict.
Check for env vars baked into local builds (`.env.local`) not present in CI.
Increase verbosity: pass `--verbose` or set CI=true to enable diagnostic flags many tools use.
tips: `npm ci` is reproducible; `npm install` may bump packages.
.env files generally shouldn't be in the repo; CI uses secrets.
Build caches in CI can mask issues — try a clean run to confirm.

triggers: works on mac fails on linux
guides.title: Cross-platform: works on Mac, fails on Linux
steps: Case sensitivity: macOS is usually case-insensitive; Linux is strict. Fix any case-mismatched imports/paths.
Line endings: macOS uses LF (good), Windows CRLF can sneak in via Git config — set `core.autocrlf` correctly.
GNU vs BSD coreutils: `sed`, `awk`, `xargs` flags differ. Use `gsed`/`gawk` locally or write POSIX-only.
File paths: hard-coded `/Users/...` won't exist on Linux. Use env vars or relative paths.
Permissions: Linux is stricter; ensure executables have +x and aren't on noexec mounts.
Test in Docker (linux container) before pushing — avoid all surprises.
tips: GNU sed in-place: `sed -i 's/x/y/' file`. BSD/Mac requires: `sed -i '' 's/x/y/' file`. Painful.
Filesystem case-insensitivity on Mac hides 'should-fail' imports — Linux exposes them.
A Linux dev container in VS Code reproduces CI locally with minimal setup.

guides.title: Encoding: UTF-8 / BOM issues
steps: Detect a BOM: `head -c 3 file | xxd` — `efbbbf` is the BOM.
Strip a BOM: `sed -i '1s/^\xEF\xBB\xBF//' file` (GNU sed) or rewrite the file in your editor without BOM.
Detect encoding: `file -i file.txt` shows it.
Convert encoding: `iconv -f WINDOWS-1252 -t UTF-8 in.txt > out.txt`.
If parsing JSON/YAML, a BOM causes 'unexpected character' errors at column 1.
Set editor to 'UTF-8 without BOM' for source files.
tips: Windows Notepad adds a BOM by default — switch tools.
YAML and JSON spec forbid BOMs — many parsers tolerate them, some don't.
VS Code: bottom bar shows encoding; click to re-save without BOM.

guides.title: General: time zone bug
steps: First rule: store all times as UTC. Convert only at display time.
Identify where the time is coming from: DB, API, system clock.
Check the server's TZ: `date` and `cat /etc/timezone`.
Set TZ explicitly in your runtime (TZ env var, container, etc.) — UTC for servers is standard.
When formatting for users, convert to their TZ at the boundary, not in the middle of logic.
If date appears 'one day off', it's often a UTC midnight crossing — check the time component too.
tips: Beware: JS `new Date('2024-01-01')` parses as UTC; `new Date('2024-01-01T00:00')` as LOCAL. Subtle.
Always test around DST transitions — bugs hide there.
Use libraries (luxon, date-fns-tz, pytz) instead of rolling your own TZ math.

guides.title: General: off-by-one error
steps: Print the boundaries: start, end, length, what's at index 0 and at index length-1.
Identify the language's slice semantics: most are half-open ([start, end)).
Sketch a small example by hand for n=0, n=1, n=2 — see when it breaks.
Common: confusing length with last index (length is N, last index is N-1).
Common: using `<=` where you meant `<` (or vice versa).
Common: iterating one beyond a sentinel that should stop you.
tips: Prefer iterators (`for x in xs`) over manual indices when possible.
Write a test for empty input, single element, and 'standard' cases — off-by-ones surface here.
Fence-post problem: N posts make N-1 fence sections.

guides.title: General: intermittent / flaky test
steps: Run it many times: `for i in 1..100; pytest -x test_foo.py`. Get a real failure rate.
Identify the category: time/async race, ordering dependence, shared resource, randomness.
Fix async races: await every promise; remove arbitrary sleeps in favor of proper waits.
Fix order dependence: isolate state, run tests in random order to expose.
Fix shared resources: unique ports, unique DB schemas per test, clean up always.
Pin random seeds at test boundaries.
tips: Quarantine, then fix — don't merge new code on a flaky baseline.
Retries hide flakiness; only use them as a temporary measure.
If a test passes alone but fails in suite, it's almost always shared state.

guides.title: General: env var not loading
steps: Confirm the file is named exactly `.env` (no extension, hidden) in the right directory.
Confirm your framework loads it: Next.js auto-loads from project root; Node needs `dotenv` imported FIRST.
Import order matters: `require('dotenv').config()` MUST be before any code that reads `process.env`.
For deployment, set env vars in the platform (Vercel, Heroku, Docker) — `.env` files often aren't deployed.
Print to verify: `console.log('X=', process.env.MY_VAR)` early in startup.
Reserved-prefix gotchas: CRA needs `REACT_APP_`; Vite needs `VITE_`; Next.js needs `NEXT_PUBLIC_` for client-side.
tips: Don't commit `.env` — add to .gitignore. Commit `.env.example` with empty values as documentation.
Trailing whitespace and quotes in env values cause silent bugs — strip both.
`direnv` auto-loads .env when you cd in — great for terminals.

guides.title: Build: Node version mismatch
steps: Read `engines` in package.json — it specifies required Node range.
Check your version: `node -v` and your CI's version.
Install the matching version: `nvm install <version> && nvm use <version>`.
Add a `.nvmrc` file with the version so collaborators auto-switch.
In CI, pin: `actions/setup-node@v4` with `node-version-file: '.nvmrc'`.
Reinstall deps after switching: `rm -rf node_modules && npm ci`.
tips: `engines` in package.json is documentation; npm doesn't enforce unless you set `engine-strict=true`.
Lockfile resolution can change with Node version — `npm ci` failures often trace here.
Volta is an alternative to nvm — auto-switches per project.

guides.title: Mobile: site broken on phone
steps: Confirm meta viewport is set: `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">`.
Open Chrome DevTools → device toolbar (Cmd+Shift+M) to simulate phones.
Inspect overflow: 100vw containers + scrollbars cause horizontal scroll. Use `max-width: 100%`.
Check fixed pixel widths in CSS — switch to %, rem, or vw/vh.
Touch targets too small: minimum 44x44px per Apple HIG.
Test on a real device — emulators miss touch and font-rendering issues.
tips: Safari iOS has its own quirks — test there too, not just Chrome's emulator.
100vh on iOS Safari includes the URL bar — use `dvh` (dynamic) or JS fallback.
BrowserStack/Sauce Labs let you test real devices remotely.

guides.title: Deploy: SPA routes 404 on refresh
steps: Recognize: the URL works when you navigate from the home page, but refresh on a deep link 404s.
Reason: the server tries to serve `/some/route` as a file, doesn't find it, returns 404.
Configure the server to serve `index.html` for ALL routes (SPA fallback).
Apache: `.htaccess` with `FallbackResource /index.html`.
Nginx: `try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html;`.
Static hosts (Netlify, Vercel) usually have a SPA toggle or `_redirects` / `vercel.json` config.
tips: Netlify: add `_redirects` with `/* /index.html 200`.
Vercel/Next.js: routing is handled, but for static export ensure rewrites.
Hash-based routing (`#/path`) sidesteps this entirely but isn't SEO-friendly.

guides.title: General: missing logs in production
steps: Check the log level: `LOG_LEVEL=info` or similar. Many frameworks default to warn/error in prod.
Make sure your log calls match: `logger.info(...)` won't appear if level is `warn`.
Confirm logs are flushed: synchronous on startup/shutdown, async during runtime.
Check where logs go: stdout, file, log service. Some platforms only capture stdout.
If using JSON logging, ensure your viewer can parse the structure.
For ephemeral containers, ship logs to a central service — they're gone on restart.
tips: 12-factor: log to stdout, let the platform handle aggregation.
Buffered logging can drop the last messages on crash — use sync logging at shutdown.
Sentry/Datadog/CloudWatch all work — pick one before you're firefighting.

guides.title: General: CRLF line endings break shell scripts
steps: Recognize the symptom: 'bad interpreter: No such file or directory' or `^M` in error output.
Confirm with `file script.sh` — 'with CRLF line terminators' is the giveaway.
Convert: `dos2unix script.sh` (if installed), or `sed -i 's/\r$//' script.sh`.
Configure git to use LF in repo: in `.gitattributes` add `*.sh text eol=lf`.
Set Git globally: `git config --global core.autocrlf input` on Linux/Mac; `true` on Windows.
Renormalize: `git add --renormalize . && git commit -m 'normalize line endings'`.
tips: Editors on Windows default to CRLF; force LF via editor settings or .editorconfig.
.editorconfig: `end_of_line = lf` is the durable answer.
WSL plus mounted Windows drives is a common source of mixed endings.

guides.title: General: it worked yesterday, broken today
steps: What changed? List every variable: code, deps, OS update, certificate expiry, time of day, DST switch.
If code changed, `git log --since=yesterday` shows commits. `git bisect` if many.
If deps changed: `npm ls --depth=0` or `pip freeze` — diff against yesterday's snapshot.
If env changed: a system update, an OS upgrade, a TLS cert expiry, a token rotation.
If time-based: DST switches, midnight UTC crossings, monthly cert renewals.
If nothing 'changed', check disk, memory, free file handles — silent resource exhaustion.
tips: git bisect is gold for code regressions — it finds the exact bad commit in log(N) steps.
TLS cert expiry is the #1 cause of 'nothing changed and it broke'.
Snapshot deps with a lockfile so 'what changed' is answerable.

guides.title: Git: clone slow or fails
steps: Try a shallow clone: `git clone --depth 1 <url>` — only latest commit.
If specific branch: `git clone --depth 1 --branch <name> <url>`.
If hanging on resolving deltas, raise buffer: `git config --global http.postBuffer 524288000`.
If a huge repo, try partial clone: `git clone --filter=blob:none <url>`.
Check network — try fetching one file from the repo via curl.
If SSH, try HTTPS as an alternative (or vice versa).
tips: Shallow clones can't push easily — unshallow with `git fetch --unshallow` if needed.
Some networks throttle long-lived TCP — pause/resume by checking out shallowly first.
Mirrors (e.g. GitHub Enterprise + LFS proxy) sometimes are faster than the canonical host.

guides.title: Python: making sense of a long traceback
steps: Read from the BOTTOM — the most useful line is the last exception type and message.
Walk up frame-by-frame: each entry is a stack level, the topmost is where Python started.
Look for the first frame in YOUR code (skip library internals).
If you see 'During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred', the lower one is the trigger; the upper is the cascade.
Use `traceback.print_exc()` in catch blocks to capture the full chain.
For exceptions in threads, install a `threading.excepthook` to surface them.
tips: rich (`pip install rich`) pretty-prints tracebacks with locals — game-changer for debugging.
Chained exceptions use `from`: `raise NewError(...) from original_err` preserves context cleanly.
`sys.exception()` in 3.11+ gets the current exception without explicit args.

guides.title: General: no space left on device
steps: Check disk usage: `df -h` — find the full filesystem.
If filesystem isn't full but you still get the error, check inodes: `df -i`.
Find big stuff: `du -sh /* 2>/dev/null | sort -h` (top-level), drill down into the biggest.
Common culprits: logs (`/var/log`), Docker (`/var/lib/docker`), build caches, node_modules everywhere.
Clean Docker: `docker system prune -a`.
Clean homebrew caches, npm caches, pip caches as appropriate.
tips: `ncdu` is an interactive du — much faster to navigate.
Lots of tiny files = inode exhaustion even with disk space free.
Truncate, don't delete, active log files: `truncate -s 0 file.log` keeps the file handle alive.

guides.title: General: too many open files
steps: Check current limit: `ulimit -n`.
Raise it for this shell: `ulimit -n 65535`.
Persist: in `/etc/security/limits.conf` add `* soft nofile 65535` (and hard).
On macOS, add `kern.maxfiles` and `kern.maxfilesperproc` to `/etc/sysctl.conf` or a launchd plist.
Find the leak in your app: not closing sockets/files in a loop. Use `lsof -p <pid>` to see what's open.
Most languages have explicit close calls or context managers — use them rigorously.
tips: 1024 is the default on many systems — way too low for any real server.
Connection pools that don't release connections are a classic leak.
Each TCP connection = one file descriptor.

guides.title: Python/pytest: print statements not showing
steps: By default pytest captures stdout. Disable with `pytest -s`.
Or run with `--capture=no` for the same effect explicitly.
On failure, captured output is shown by default — only on PASS is it hidden.
If you really need real-time output, `-s --log-cli-level=DEBUG`.
Use `caplog` fixture to inspect captured logs in assertions.
Use `capsys` fixture to inspect captured stdout/stderr in assertions.
tips: `-s` is the most-used pytest flag for interactive debugging.
If you need a debugger, `pytest --pdb` drops into pdb on failure.
`pytest -x` stops at the first failure — great for iterating.

guides.title: JS: works in dev, fails in prod (devDependency)
steps: Check the failing import — is the package in `dependencies` or `devDependencies`?
Production installs (`npm ci --production`, `NODE_ENV=production npm install`) skip devDependencies.
If the package is needed at runtime, move it to `dependencies`: `npm install <pkg> --save`.
If it's only build-time, ensure your build step runs before pruning devDeps.
For Docker: keep devDeps during build stage, prune in final stage.
Verify with `npm ls <pkg>` — should show it as not-dev-only.
tips: Common mistake: TypeScript/babel in devDeps, runtime helpers also there. Move runtime helpers out.
`npm prune --production` removes devDeps from an existing install — useful after build.
Multi-stage Docker: build in one stage with all deps, copy to slim runtime stage.

guides.title: General: pipe terminal output to clipboard
steps: macOS: `echo hello | pbcopy` — clipboard now has 'hello'. Paste with `pbpaste`.
Linux X11: install xclip, then `echo hello | xclip -selection clipboard`.
Linux Wayland: `wl-copy` and `wl-paste`.
Windows (Git Bash): `echo hello | clip.exe`.
WSL: `echo hello | clip.exe` reaches the Windows clipboard.
Make it a function: `alias clip='pbcopy'` (or distro equivalent) for muscle memory.
tips: Tmux 'copy mode' captures terminal output into its own buffer — sync to system clipboard with config.
iTerm2 (Mac) can auto-copy on selection — saves keystrokes.
`pbpaste | command` is great for processing whatever you copied.

guides.title: Python: sys.path / PYTHONPATH issues
steps: Print sys.path: `python -c 'import sys; print(sys.path)'`. Note your cwd is usually `''` in the list.
If your local module isn't on sys.path, run from the project root, or add `PYTHONPATH=src python ...`.
Better: install your package in editable mode: `pip install -e .` with a `pyproject.toml`.
Or use `python -m mymodule` instead of `python path/to/mymodule.py` — the `-m` adds the package's root to sys.path correctly.
Add `__init__.py` to make a folder a real package (or PEP 420 namespace if you skip it).
Avoid mucking with `sys.path` from your code — fix the install instead.
tips: `pip install -e .` is the right way to make local imports work — no path hacks needed.
`python -m` is much more reliable than running scripts directly for path resolution.
Layout matters: src layout vs flat layout has different gotchas.

guides.title: JS/React: too many re-renders
steps: Read the error: 'Maximum update depth exceeded' or 'Too many re-renders'.
Look for state updates IN render: calling `setX()` directly in the function body re-runs render forever.
Move state updates into event handlers or useEffect.
Check useEffect deps: an object/array in deps recreated each render triggers infinite effects. Memoize with useMemo or extract primitives.
Check that event handlers aren't called by mistake (e.g. `onClick={handler()}` calls; `onClick={handler}` references).
Add `console.log('render')` at the top of the component to count renders.
Use React DevTools Profiler to see what's re-rendering.
tips: Most infinite-render bugs are 'I called setX during render' — search for setX outside callbacks.
An object literal in deps `[{ foo: 1 }]` is a new reference every render — useMemo it.
useCallback for handlers passed to memoized children.

guides.title: Python: PicklingError
steps: Read the error — it names what can't be pickled (often a lambda, local function, or thread lock).
Replace lambdas with top-level functions.
Don't pass module-level resources (open files, connections) across processes — open them in the worker.
For `multiprocessing`, switch to `dill` (`import dill as pickle`) which handles more cases — or use `multiprocess` library.
For `concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor`, the same restriction applies.
Consider switching to threads if the work is I/O bound and pickling is the blocker.
tips: Pickling rules: top-level callables only, no open OS handles, no thread locks.
`__reduce__` lets you define how a class pickles if needed.
Cloudpickle (used by Dask, Ray) is broader than stdlib pickle — sometimes a drop-in fix.

guides.title: Python/Jupyter: kernel keeps dying
steps: Open the terminal that launched Jupyter — kernel crashes log there.
If OOM, free memory or downsize data. Check with `htop`.
If a native lib segfaults, isolate which import — comment out and run a minimal cell.
Numpy/scipy/torch built against different BLAS can crash on import — match versions.
On Apple Silicon, mixed arm64/x86 wheels can crash — reinstall everything for one architecture.
Update ipykernel: `pip install --upgrade ipykernel`.
tips: Kernel logs are in `~/.jupyter` or printed to the launching terminal — check both.
If it crashes on import, that import is incompatible with another in the env.
Fresh venv + reinstall is faster than tracking down a binary mismatch.

guides.title: Git: track a remote branch
steps: On a new local branch, first push: `git push -u origin <branch>` sets upstream and pushes.
For an existing branch: `git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/<branch>`.
Confirm: `git branch -vv` shows tracking info per branch.
After upstream is set, `git push` and `git pull` work without args.
To switch what a branch tracks: `git branch --set-upstream-to=<new-remote>/<new-branch>`.
tips: `push.autoSetupRemote=true` in config means `git push` of a new branch sets upstream automatically.
`git fetch` updates remote-tracking refs (origin/main) without touching your local branches.
`git remote -v` shows the URL behind each remote name.

guides.title: Network: intermittent / flaky connectivity
steps: Run `mtr <host>` for a few minutes — it pings AND traceroutes continuously, showing packet loss per hop.
If loss appears at a specific hop, that hop is the problem.
Test at different times — ISP congestion has patterns.
Test from a different network (phone hotspot) to isolate your network vs the destination.
Check DNS resolver — sometimes DNS times out while reachability is fine: `dig +stats <host>`.
If wireless, test wired to isolate Wi-Fi as cause.
tips: `mtr` is the single best tool for intermittent issues — better than ping or traceroute alone.
Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 or Google's 8.8.8.8 as a test DNS isolates resolver issues.
Wi-Fi interference (2.4 GHz especially) is wildly underestimated as a cause.

guides.title: Python: new-feature syntax errors on old Python
steps: Confirm Python version: `python --version`.
Map: walrus `:=` needs 3.8+; positional-only `/` needs 3.8+; `match` needs 3.10+; PEP 695 generics need 3.12+; type statements need 3.12+.
f-strings need 3.6+; nested f-strings with quotes need 3.12+.
If supporting old versions, rewrite without the feature OR raise the minimum.
Set `python_requires` in setup.cfg/pyproject.toml to enforce.
Use `pyupgrade` to add new syntax automatically once you bump the minimum.
tips: End-of-life Pythons (3.7 and older) are commonly broken — drop support unless required.
ruff/mypy can be configured to your minimum version and warn on incompatible usage.
vermin scans a codebase for the minimum Python version actually required by the syntax used.

guides.title: JS: silent promise / async failure
steps: Find the async call — look for a missing `await` or `.catch`.
Wrap awaits in try/catch: `try { await x() } catch (e) { ... }`.
Chain `.catch()` on every promise where you don't have try/catch.
In Node, install a global handler: `process.on('unhandledRejection', e => console.error(e))`.
In the browser: `window.addEventListener('unhandledrejection', e => ...)`.
Forgot to return a promise from an arrow body? `() => asyncFn()` returns the promise; `() => { asyncFn() }` swallows it.
tips: Implicit-return arrows propagate the inner promise; block-body arrows need explicit `return`.
ESLint's `no-floating-promises` (TypeScript-ESLint) catches every dangling promise.
Top-level await in ESM removes a lot of swallow-prone patterns.

guides.title: Network: debugging an HTTP request with curl
steps: Start with `-v`: `curl -v https://api.example.com/path` — shows TLS, headers, response.
Show only response headers: `curl -I <url>`.
Save body to a file: `curl -o body.json <url>` so the terminal isn't flooded.
Send custom headers: `-H 'Authorization: Bearer X' -H 'Content-Type: application/json'`.
POST JSON: `-X POST -d '{"k":"v"}' -H 'Content-Type: application/json'`.
Follow redirects: `-L`. Trace timings: `-w '%{time_total}\n' -o /dev/null -s`.
tips: `httpie` is a friendlier alternative for ad-hoc testing.
`curl --trace-ascii /dev/stdout` shows every byte sent and received — nuclear option.
`-w` format strings give you precise timing breakdowns (DNS, TLS, TTFB, total).

guides.title: Tracking down a Python ImportError / ModuleNotFoundError
steps: Read the full traceback bottom-up: the last line names the exact module Python could not find, not necessarily the one you typed.
Run `python -c "import sys; print(sys.path)"` and confirm the directory holding your package is actually on the path.
Check you launched the script the way the imports expect: `python -m package.module` from the project root resolves package-relative imports that `python package/module.py` does not.
Verify there is an `__init__.py` (or you're on Python 3.3+ namespace packages) in every folder you import through.
Make sure your file isn't shadowing a real module (a local `random.py` or `email.py` will hijack the stdlib import).
Confirm you installed into the same interpreter you're running with `python -m pip list` rather than a globally aliased `pip`.
If it's a third-party package, reinstall into the active venv and re-run.
tips: `pip list` and `python` pointing at different environments is the #1 cause; always prefer `python -m pip`.
A circular import shows up as ImportError on a name that exists — split the shared code into a third module.

guides.title: Debugging a misbehaving Python virtual environment
steps: Run `which python` (or `where python` on Windows) and confirm it points inside your venv's `bin`/`Scripts` folder.
Check the venv is actually active: your prompt should show its name, and `echo $VIRTUAL_ENV` should print the path.
Run `python -m pip --version` and verify the pip path is inside the same venv, not a system location.
If packages are 'missing', run `python -m pip list` inside the venv to see what's truly installed there.
Recreate the venv if its interpreter symlink broke after an OS Python upgrade: `python -m venv --clear .venv`.
Reinstall dependencies with `python -m pip install -r requirements.txt` after reactivating.
tips: Editors often cache a stale interpreter — reselect the venv interpreter in your IDE after creating it.
Never `sudo pip install` inside a venv; it writes to system site-packages and breaks isolation.

guides.title: Fixing 'AttributeError: NoneType object has no attribute'
steps: Note the attribute name in the error — it tells you what you tried to call on a value that turned out to be None.
Find the assignment that produced that variable and check whether the function on its right returns None on some path.
Look for the classic trap: `x = mylist.sort()` or `x = mydict.update()` — these mutate in place and return None.
Check for a function missing an explicit `return`, which silently returns None.
Add a `print(repr(var))` or breakpoint right before the failing line to confirm it's None and trace back.
Guard the call with an explicit check (`if var is not None:`) or fix the upstream function to return the value.
tips: `.sort()`, `.append()`, `.reverse()` all return None — chain off the original object instead.
A regex `.match()` returns None when there's no match; check before calling `.group()`.

guides.title: Diagnosing a Python KeyError
steps: Read the KeyError message — the value shown is the exact key that was missing.
Print the dict's actual keys with `print(list(d.keys()))` right before the failing access to compare.
Watch for whitespace, case, or type mismatches: the string `'1'` and the int `1` are different keys.
If the key is optional, switch to `d.get(key, default)` instead of `d[key]`.
For deeply nested data (like JSON), check each level exists rather than assuming the whole path.
If you're building the dict, confirm the key was actually set before this point — a typo in the setter is common.
tips: `collections.defaultdict` auto-creates missing keys if absence is expected behavior.
JSON numbers parse to int/float, but JSON object keys are always strings — `data['5']` not `data[5]`.

guides.title: Clearing up Python IndentationError and TabError
steps: Read the line number in the error; the real problem is often the line just above it.
Check whether you mixed tabs and spaces — a TabError means inconsistent whitespace within a block.
Turn on 'show whitespace' / 'render control characters' in your editor to see tabs vs spaces visually.
Confirm every `if/for/def/while/with/try` header is followed by an indented body.
Re-indent the offending block uniformly with spaces (PEP 8 = 4 spaces) using your editor's convert-tabs-to-spaces.
Run `python -m tabnanny yourfile.py` to have Python pinpoint ambiguous indentation.
tips: Set your editor to insert spaces for the Tab key project-wide to avoid this entirely.
Copy-pasting from the web or PDFs often injects non-breaking spaces that look like normal spaces but aren't.

guides.title: Resolving a Python TypeError about function arguments
steps: Read whether it's 'missing N required positional arguments' or 'takes N but N were given' — they point opposite directions.
Compare the function/method definition's parameter list against the actual call site.
For method calls, remember `self` is implicit; calling `Class.method(x)` instead of `instance.method(x)` shifts every argument.
Check you didn't forget to pass an argument or accidentally pass an extra one via unpacking (`*args`/`**kwargs`).
If you decorated the function, confirm the decorator preserves the signature (use `functools.wraps`).
Add the keyword names explicitly (`fn(width=3, height=4)`) to make a mismatch obvious.
tips: Calling a function but forgetting `()` passes the function object itself, often triggering this later.
A bound method counts its instance as the first argument — don't pass it again.

guides.title: Fixing 'IndexError: list index out of range'
steps: Print the length of the sequence right before the failing access with `print(len(seq))`.
Compare that length to the index you're using — accessing `seq[len(seq)]` is always one too far.
If it's in a loop, check your range bounds: `range(len(seq))` is correct, `range(len(seq)+1)` overshoots.
Watch for an empty sequence: `seq[0]` on `[]` always fails — guard with `if seq:`.
For nested indexing, confirm the inner list is as long as you expect, not just the outer.
Iterate directly (`for item in seq`) or use `enumerate` instead of manual indexing to sidestep the bug.
tips: Negative indices wrap, but `seq[-len(seq)-1]` still overflows the other way.
Mutating a list while iterating by index shifts everything and produces phantom out-of-range hits.

guides.title: Debugging the mutable default argument trap
steps: Notice the symptom: a list/dict default keeps data from previous calls instead of starting fresh.
Inspect the signature for `def f(items=[])` or `def f(opts={})` — the default is created once at definition time, not per call.
Confirm by calling the function twice and printing the argument; it accumulates across calls.
Change the default to `None`: `def f(items=None):`.
Inside the body, set `if items is None: items = []` so each call gets a fresh object.
Re-run your repeated-call test and confirm each invocation starts clean.
tips: This applies to any mutable default: lists, dicts, sets, and instances.
Linters like Ruff/Pylint flag this as B006 — enable it to catch the pattern automatically.

guides.title: Solving a Python UnicodeDecodeError when reading files
steps: Read which byte position and codec the error names — `0x80`-`0xFF` bytes usually mean the file isn't UTF-8.
Determine the file's real encoding: try `file yourfile.txt` on Unix, or open it in an editor that reports encoding.
Pass the correct encoding explicitly: `open(path, encoding='latin-1')` or `'cp1252'` for Windows-origin text.
If you only need bytes, open in binary mode (`'rb'`) and decode deliberately where you control errors.
As a last resort for messy data, use `errors='replace'` or `errors='ignore'` to keep going while logging the loss.
For mystery files, install and run `chardet`/`charset-normalizer` to guess the encoding.
tips: Never rely on the platform default encoding — always pass `encoding=` explicitly for portability.
A UTF-8 BOM appears as `\ufeff`; open with `encoding='utf-8-sig'` to strip it.

guides.title: Debugging a Python RecursionError
steps: Confirm the function actually has a base case that returns without recursing.
Check that each recursive call moves toward the base case (the argument must shrink or change).
Print the argument at the top of the function to watch whether it's converging or stuck.
Look for two functions that call each other indirectly forming an unintended cycle.
If the recursion is legitimately deep but finite, raise the limit with `sys.setrecursionlimit(N)` cautiously.
For very deep logic, rewrite the recursion as an explicit loop with a stack to avoid the limit entirely.
tips: A property that references itself (`self.x` returning `self.x`) recurses forever — common typo.
`__getattr__` or `__repr__` accidentally accessing the same attribute it defines causes silent infinite recursion.

guides.title: Fixing 'ValueError: too many/not enough values to unpack'
steps: Read whether it's 'too many' or 'not enough' — that tells you which side has the wrong count.
Count the names on the left of the `=` and compare to the actual length of the right-hand value.
Print the right-hand value with `print(repr(value))` to see exactly how many items it holds.
Watch for a single-item line being treated as multiple, e.g. unpacking a string into characters.
When the count varies, use starred unpacking: `first, *rest = items` to absorb the remainder.
If iterating, confirm each element has the structure you assume (e.g. `for k, v in pairs` needs 2-tuples).
tips: `a, b = somefunc()` fails if the function sometimes returns a single value instead of a tuple.
Splitting a line with no delimiter returns a one-element list — guard `key, val = line.split('=')`.

guides.title: Debugging f-strings that don't interpolate
steps: Confirm the string literal actually starts with `f` (or `F`) before the opening quote.
Check you're not on Python 2 or a pre-3.6 interpreter where f-strings don't exist (you'd get a SyntaxError instead).
If braces print literally, you likely doubled them (`{{}}`) — single braces interpolate, doubles are escapes.
Verify the names inside the braces are actually in scope at that point in the code.
For nested quotes in older versions, use a different quote style inside the expression to avoid clashes.
If using `.format()` instead, ensure placeholders `{}` match the arguments passed.
tips: Logging with `logging.info('x=%s', x)` is preferred over f-strings so the format only runs when the level is enabled.
An f-string with no `{}` is just a normal string — no error, but a sign you forgot the placeholder.

guides.title: Diagnosing json.JSONDecodeError
steps: Read the line/column in the error and inspect that exact spot in the raw text.
Print or log the raw string you're parsing — it's often an HTML error page or empty body, not JSON.
'Expecting value: line 1 column 1' usually means an empty string or a leading byte-order mark.
'Extra data' means you have multiple JSON objects concatenated; parse line-by-line (JSON Lines) instead.
Check for single quotes, trailing commas, or Python `None`/`True` — valid Python, invalid JSON.
If reading a file, confirm you passed the file contents (or a file object to `json.load`) and not the path string.
tips: `json.loads` takes a string; `json.load` takes a file object — mixing them is a common slip.
API responses can be gzipped or non-200; check status and content-type before decoding.

guides.title: Fixing 'changed size during iteration' / loop-mutation bugs
steps: Identify the loop that both iterates over a collection and adds/removes items from it.
For dicts/sets, the RuntimeError is explicit; for lists, mutation silently skips elements instead.
Iterate over a copy: `for x in list(items):` or `for k in list(d.keys()):` so the original can change safely.
Better, build a new collection: use a comprehension to keep only the items you want.
For deletion, collect keys/indices to remove first, then delete them in a second pass.
Re-run and confirm every intended element was processed.
tips: Deleting by index in a forward loop shifts later items left, so the next one gets skipped.
`filter`/comprehensions are usually clearer and safer than in-place mutation.

guides.title: Debugging unexpected results from Python division and rounding
steps: Decide whether you want true division (`/`, always float) or floor division (`//`, rounds toward negative infinity).
Print the operand types — mixing ints and floats changes the result type and precision.
For money or exact decimals, switch from `float` to `decimal.Decimal` to avoid binary float drift (0.1+0.2).
Check `round()` behavior: Python uses banker's rounding (round-half-to-even), so `round(2.5)` is 2.
For negative numbers, remember `-7 // 2 == -4` and `-7 % 2 == 1` — modulo follows the divisor's sign.
Reproduce with the exact inputs in a REPL to confirm the operator, not the data, is the issue.
tips: Never compare floats with `==`; use `math.isclose(a, b)`.
`Decimal('0.1')` from a string is exact; `Decimal(0.1)` from a float inherits the float's error.

guides.title: Resolving UnboundLocalError and scope confusion
steps: Read the variable named in 'referenced before assignment' — it's being treated as local.
Check whether you assign to that name anywhere in the function; any assignment makes it local for the whole function.
If you meant to read a module-level variable and also reassign it, add `global name` at the top of the function.
For an enclosing function's variable, use `nonlocal name` instead of `global`.
If you only need to read it, remove the accidental assignment or rename the local.
For closures created in a loop, bind the current value with a default argument (`lambda x=x: ...`) to avoid late binding.
tips: `x += 1` counts as an assignment, so it makes `x` local even though it also reads it first.
Loop variables in comprehensions are scoped to the comprehension in Python 3 — they don't leak.

guides.title: Breaking a Python circular import
steps: Read the error — 'cannot import name X' or 'partially initialized module' signals a circular dependency.
Trace the import chain: module A imports B at top level, and B imports A, forming a loop.
Identify the shared name both modules need and consider moving it into a third, dependency-free module.
If the import is only needed inside a function, move it to a local (deferred) import to break the top-level cycle.
Reorganize so dependencies flow one direction (low-level modules don't import high-level ones).
Re-run from a clean interpreter to confirm the cycle is gone (stale `.pyc` can mask it).
tips: Type-only imports can go under `if TYPE_CHECKING:` to avoid runtime cycles.
Importing the module (`import b`) and using `b.thing` is more cycle-tolerant than `from b import thing`.

guides.title: Debugging asserts that never fire
steps: Check whether Python was started with `-O` (optimize), which strips all `assert` statements entirely.
Confirm `__debug__` is True in your environment: `python -c "print(__debug__)"`.
Verify you didn't write `assert (cond, msg)` — a parenthesized tuple is always truthy and never fails.
Make sure the assert is on a reachable line and the condition is actually False when you expect a failure.
If the check must run in production, replace the assert with an explicit `if not cond: raise ValueError(...)`.
Re-run without `-O` to confirm the assert triggers as designed.
tips: `assert x, 'msg'` is correct; `assert (x, 'msg')` is the silent bug — note the comma inside parens.
Never use asserts for input validation that matters; treat them as dev-only sanity checks.

guides.title: Debugging Python datetime timezone issues
steps: Check whether your datetimes are naive (no tzinfo) or aware — comparing the two raises a TypeError.
Print `dt.tzinfo` on each value to see which ones carry timezone info.
Standardize on timezone-aware UTC internally: `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` instead of `datetime.now()`.
Convert for display only at the edges with `.astimezone(zoneinfo.ZoneInfo('America/New_York'))`.
When parsing strings, attach the correct tzinfo rather than assuming local time.
Re-run arithmetic/comparisons once both sides are aware and in a consistent zone.
tips: `datetime.utcnow()` returns a naive datetime even though it's UTC — prefer `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`.
Use `zoneinfo` (stdlib 3.9+) over `pytz`; pytz needs `.localize()` and behaves differently.

guides.title: Debugging a failing pip install
steps: Read the final error block, not the first warning — 'could not build wheel' vs 'no matching distribution' need different fixes.
'No matching distribution' means the package/version doesn't exist for your Python version or platform; check `python --version` against the package's requirements.
'Failed building wheel' usually means missing system build tools or headers; install the compiler/dev packages or look for a prebuilt wheel.
For dependency conflicts, read which two packages disagree and pin a compatible pair, or use a fresh venv.
Permission-denied errors mean you're installing into system Python — use a venv or `--user`, never `sudo`.
Upgrade pip itself (`python -m pip install -U pip`) since old pip can't read newer package metadata.
Re-run with `-v` for verbose output if the cause is still unclear.
tips: A corporate proxy or firewall causes timeouts that masquerade as 'package not found'.
Pin versions in requirements.txt so a transitive upgrade doesn't break a clean install later.

guides.title: Debugging shared-reference (shallow vs deep copy) bugs
steps: Confirm the symptom: changing one list/dict mysteriously changes another that should be separate.
Check the assignment — `b = a` makes b an alias of a, not a copy; they're the same object.
Verify with `print(a is b)`; if True, they share identity and every mutation is shared.
For a flat structure, make a shallow copy: `b = a.copy()` or `b = list(a)`.
For nested structures, a shallow copy still shares the inner objects — use `copy.deepcopy(a)`.
Re-test by mutating one and confirming the other is untouched.
tips: `[[0]*3]*3` creates three references to the SAME inner list — use a comprehension instead.
Default function arguments and class attributes that are mutable get shared across instances.

guides.title: Debugging an exhausted generator/iterator
steps: Confirm the symptom: the first loop over the value works, but a second loop yields nothing.
Check whether the value is a generator or iterator (`map`, `filter`, `zip`, `(x for x in ...)`), which can only be consumed once.
Print `type(value)` — if it's a generator or one of the lazy builtins, exhaustion is the cause.
If you need to iterate more than once, materialize it: `items = list(generator)` and loop over the list.
If memory matters and you must keep it lazy, recreate the generator each time you need a fresh pass.
Re-run both loops and confirm the data appears each time.
tips: `zip`, `map`, and `filter` return one-shot iterators in Python 3, not lists.
Passing a generator to `len()` fails; convert to a list/tuple first if you need a count.

guides.title: Debugging Python string/identity comparison bugs
steps: Check whether you're using `is` instead of `==`; `is` tests identity, not value, and only happens to work for small interned strings/ints.
Switch value comparisons to `==` and reserve `is` for `None`, `True`, `False`.
Print `repr()` of both strings to reveal hidden differences: trailing spaces, newlines, or `\r`.
Normalize before comparing: `.strip()` for whitespace and `.lower()`/`.casefold()` for case.
Watch for Unicode normalization — visually identical strings can have different code points; apply `unicodedata.normalize('NFC', s)`.
Re-run the comparison after normalizing both sides.
tips: `a is b` working in the REPL for short strings is interning luck — it breaks for longer/computed strings.
Reading a file line keeps the trailing `\n`; strip it before comparing to a constant.

guides.title: Diagnosing MemoryError / OOM when processing large data
steps: Confirm whether it's a true MemoryError or the OS killing the process (check dmesg / exit code 137).
Find the line building the largest structure — usually a `list()` over a huge file or a giant comprehension.
Stream instead of loading: iterate the file line-by-line (`for line in f:`) rather than `f.readlines()`.
Replace eager comprehensions feeding `sum`/`any`/`max` with generator expressions (drop the brackets).
Process in chunks (e.g. pandas `chunksize=`, or batched reads) instead of one giant object.
Profile with `tracemalloc` or `memory_profiler` to confirm where allocation peaks.
tips: Exit code 137 (128+9) means SIGKILL from the OOM killer — Python never raised the error itself.
`sys.getsizeof` only measures the container shell, not the referenced objects inside it.

guides.title: Debugging a Python regex that won't match
steps: Print the pattern and the input with `repr()` to see exactly what the engine receives, including escapes.
Use a raw string for the pattern (`r'\d+'`) so backslashes aren't eaten by Python's string parser first.
Check `re.match` (anchors at start) vs `re.search` (anywhere) vs `re.fullmatch` — wrong choice gives no match.
Test incrementally: simplify the pattern until it matches, then add complexity back to find the breaking piece.
Verify special characters are escaped (`.` `(` `[` `+` `*`) when you mean them literally.
Use named groups and `re.VERBOSE` for readability, and confirm `.group(n)` indexes the group you expect.
tips: `.` doesn't match newlines unless you pass `re.DOTALL`; `^`/`$` are line-bound only with `re.MULTILINE`.
Greedy `.*` can swallow too much — use `.*?` (lazy) or a more specific character class.

triggers: no such file or directory python
guides.title: Fixing FileNotFoundError when opening a file
steps: Print the current working directory with `import os; print(os.getcwd())` — relative paths resolve against it, not the script's location.
Print the exact path you passed (`print(os.path.abspath(path))`) and check it on disk.
Build paths from the script's own location with `Path(__file__).parent / 'data.csv'` to make them CWD-independent.
Check for typos, wrong case (case-sensitive on Linux/macOS), and stray spaces in the filename.
Confirm the file actually exists and you have read permission with `os.path.exists(path)` and `os.access`.
If writing, make sure the parent directory exists (`Path(p).parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)`).
tips: Running the same script from a different directory changes how relative paths resolve.
`~` is not expanded automatically — call `os.path.expanduser('~/file')` or `Path.home()`.

guides.title: Debugging Python threads that aren't speeding things up
steps: Determine if your workload is CPU-bound or I/O-bound — this decides whether threading can ever help.
Recall the GIL: only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time, so CPU-bound threads don't run in parallel.
For CPU-bound work, switch to `multiprocessing` or `concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor` to use multiple cores.
For I/O-bound work (network, disk), threads or `asyncio` do help because the GIL releases during I/O waits.
Profile to confirm where time goes (`cProfile`) before assuming parallelism is the fix.
Watch for shared-state contention; add locks only around the minimal critical section.
tips: C extensions like NumPy release the GIL during heavy math, so threading can help there even for compute.
Process pools have serialization (pickle) overhead — tiny tasks can run slower than single-threaded.

guides.title: Debugging a try/except that doesn't catch the error
steps: Read the uncaught traceback to see the actual exception class and where it was raised.
Confirm your `except` clause names that class or a base class of it — `except ValueError` won't catch a `KeyError`.
Check the error isn't raised outside the `try` block's lines (only code inside `try` is protected).
Make sure you aren't catching a narrower type while a different one is thrown.
Temporarily widen to `except Exception as e:` and `print(type(e), e)` to learn the real class, then narrow back.
Verify you're not re-raising or that a `finally`/inner handler isn't swallowing then crashing elsewhere.
tips: `except Exception` does not catch `KeyboardInterrupt` or `SystemExit` (they derive from BaseException).
A bare `except:` hides everything including typos in the handler — always catch the narrowest useful type.

guides.title: Debugging class vs instance attribute confusion
steps: Confirm the symptom: a value set on one instance appears on all instances, or changes leak between objects.
Check where the attribute is defined — assigned at class body level (class attribute) vs inside `__init__` (instance attribute).
Remember a mutable class attribute (`tags = []` in the class body) is shared by every instance.
Move per-instance state into `__init__`: `self.tags = []` so each object gets its own.
Verify with `print(InstanceA.tags is InstanceB.tags)` — True means they're sharing one object.
Re-test by mutating one instance and confirming others are unaffected.
tips: Reading a class attribute through `self` works, but assigning through `self` creates a new instance attribute that shadows it.
Use class attributes intentionally for constants/defaults, not for mutable per-instance data.

guides.title: Systematically debugging a Python logic bug with no traceback
steps: Reproduce the wrong result reliably with the smallest input that still shows it.
State the expected vs actual output precisely so you know what 'wrong' means.
Bisect the code: print or log intermediate values at the midpoint to see where reality diverges from expectation.
Drop a breakpoint with `breakpoint()` (or `import pdb; pdb.set_trace()`) and step through with n/s/c, inspecting variables.
Check assumptions about types and emptiness at the divergence point with `print(type(x), repr(x))`.
Once located, write a small failing test that captures the bug, then fix and confirm the test passes.
Remove temporary prints/breakpoints before committing.
tips: Rubber-duck the divergence point: explain aloud what each line should do versus what it does.
Prefer `logging` over scattered prints so you can flip verbosity without editing code.

guides.title: Debug "Cannot read properties of undefined"
steps: Read the full error: it names the property, like 'reading length' — that tells you which access failed.
Find the line number in the stack trace and look at the chain right before the named property (e.g. user.profile.name — one of user/profile is undefined).
Add a console.log of the object one level up from the crash, or set a breakpoint there, to see which link is undefined.
Trace backwards: where was that value assigned? Common causes are an async value not yet resolved, a missing API field, or an array .find() that returned nothing.
Guard the access with optional chaining (user?.profile?.name) or a default, then decide whether undefined is actually a bug upstream you should fix instead.
Re-run and confirm the crash is gone and the value you expected is present, not just silenced.
tips: Optional chaining hides the symptom — make sure undefined is genuinely acceptable, not a sign data never loaded.
Array methods like .find() and .pop() return undefined silently when nothing matches.

guides.title: Debug an async function that returns undefined
steps: Check that you actually awaited the call: const x = await getData(), not const x = getData() which gives you a Promise.
Inside the async function, confirm there is a return statement on the success path — a function with no return resolves to undefined.
Look for a return inside a .forEach or a plain callback; those returns do not bubble up to the outer function.
console.log the value immediately before the return and immediately after the await at the call site to see where it becomes undefined.
If you mapped promises, ensure you used await Promise.all(arr.map(...)) rather than awaiting the array of promises directly.
Verify no early return or try/catch is swallowing the result before the real return runs.
tips: An unawaited async call logs as Promise { <pending> }, not the value — that is the tell.
return inside forEach is a no-op; use a for...of loop or map when you need the values.

guides.title: Track down an UnhandledPromiseRejection
steps: Run node with --unhandled-rejections=strict (Node 15+ does this by default) so the process exits and prints a real stack.
Add a process.on('unhandledRejection', (reason) => console.error(reason)) handler temporarily to capture the reason and stack.
Scan for promise-returning calls with no await and no .catch() — those are the usual source.
Check .then() chains that have no trailing .catch(); a throw inside any .then rejects the whole chain.
Wrap the suspect await in try/catch, log the error, and confirm the warning disappears.
Decide on real handling: retry, surface to the user, or rethrow — do not just swallow it.
tips: A fire-and-forget call like doThing() (no await) is the most common cause.
In Express, async route handlers need a wrapper or .catch — Express 4 does not catch async throws for you.

guides.title: Resolve "Cannot find module" in Node
steps: Read whether the missing name is a package or a relative path — packages have no ./ prefix, files do.
If it is a package, run npm ls <name>; if missing, npm install it and check it is in package.json dependencies (not just devDependencies for production).
If it is a relative path, verify the file exists and the spelling/case match exactly — Linux is case-sensitive even when your Mac is not.
Confirm the file extension: ESM and some bundlers require the explicit .js in import paths.
Delete node_modules and package-lock.json, then npm install fresh to rule out a corrupt install.
Check you are running from the directory you think — a wrong cwd makes relative requires fail.
tips: Case mismatches pass locally on macOS/Windows but fail in CI/Docker on Linux.
If only present after deploy, the dependency is probably under devDependencies and was pruned.

guides.title: Fix ESM vs CommonJS module errors
steps: Identify the error: ERR_REQUIRE_ESM means you required an ESM-only package; 'Cannot use import outside a module' means import syntax in a CommonJS file.
Check your package.json "type" field — "module" makes .js files ESM, absent/"commonjs" makes them CommonJS.
Decide one direction: either set "type":"module" and use import everywhere, or keep CommonJS and require everywhere.
For an ESM-only dependency in a CommonJS project, switch the import to a dynamic await import('pkg') inside an async function.
Rename files to .mjs (ESM) or .cjs (CommonJS) to override the package default per file when you must mix.
Re-run and confirm both your code and the dependency load with consistent module syntax.
tips: You cannot top-level require an ESM-only package from CommonJS — use dynamic import().
__dirname and require do not exist in ESM; use import.meta.url and createRequire if needed.

guides.title: Debug "Maximum call stack size exceeded"
steps: Look at the stack trace for a short repeating cycle of the same function name(s) — that is your infinite recursion.
Find the recursive function and check its base case: confirm the condition that stops recursion is actually reachable.
Verify the recursive call moves toward the base case (e.g. n-1, smaller array) and is not passing the same value each time.
Watch for accidental recursion: a getter that reads its own property, or a toString that stringifies itself.
If recursion is legitimate but deep, rewrite it iteratively with an explicit stack or array.
Add a temporary depth counter that throws at, say, 1000 to capture the arguments when it runs away.
tips: Two functions calling each other (mutual recursion) hide the cycle — read the whole repeated block.
A property getter named the same as the backing field recurses forever — back it with a private field.

guides.title: Hunt a Node.js memory leak
steps: Confirm it is a leak, not just a big workload: log process.memoryUsage().heapUsed over time and check it trends up and never recovers after GC.
Start the process with node --inspect and open chrome://inspect, or use the heap snapshot API to capture a baseline.
Exercise the suspected path repeatedly, take a second heap snapshot, and compare — sort retained objects by size in the diff.
Look for the usual culprits: growing module-level arrays/maps, event listeners added in a loop without removal, timers never cleared, or closures holding large objects.
Fix the retention: clear collections, removeListener / clearInterval, or null out references when done.
Re-run the load and confirm heapUsed plateaus instead of climbing.
tips: EventEmitter warns 'possible memory leak' at 11 listeners — that warning often points right at the bug.
Bump the limit with --max-old-space-size only as a stopgap; it does not fix the leak.

guides.title: Fix EADDRINUSE (port already in use)
steps: Read the port number from the error message (e.g. EADDRINUSE :::3000).
Find what holds it: lsof -i :3000 on macOS/Linux, or netstat -ano | findstr :3000 on Windows.
If it is a stale copy of your own app, kill it: kill -9 <PID> (or taskkill /PID <pid> /F on Windows).
If you intentionally run multiple instances, change the port via an env var (PORT) instead of hardcoding.
Add a graceful shutdown (server.close() on SIGINT/SIGTERM) so the port frees when you stop the app.
Restart and confirm the server binds cleanly.
tips: Nodemon double-starts can orphan a process — check for a lingering node PID before assuming another app.
On macOS, port 5000 is often taken by AirPlay Receiver; pick another port or disable it.

guides.title: Debug a wrong or undefined `this`
steps: console.log(this) at the top of the misbehaving function to see what it actually is — undefined, the global, or some other object.
Identify how the function was called: a method call (obj.fn()) binds this to obj; a bare call (fn()) does not.
Check for a regular function passed as a callback (setTimeout, .map, event handler) — it loses the surrounding this.
Convert the callback to an arrow function so it captures the lexical this, OR bind it explicitly with .bind(this).
For class methods used as handlers, bind in the constructor or use a class field arrow method.
Re-run and confirm this points to the object you expect.
tips: Arrow functions have no own this — that is the fix for callbacks but wrong for object methods that need dynamic this.
'use strict' makes a bare function's this undefined instead of the global object, surfacing bugs sooner.

guides.title: Debug JSON.parse failures
steps: Read the message: 'Unexpected token o in JSON' means you passed an object (it got stringified to [object Object]); 'Unexpected end of JSON input' means empty or truncated input.
Log the raw string you are about to parse, including its length and the first/last characters, before calling JSON.parse.
Check it is actually JSON: trailing commas, single quotes, and unquoted keys are valid JS but invalid JSON.
If it comes from fetch, confirm you read the body once and the response was actually JSON (a 500 HTML error page will not parse).
Strip a possible BOM or whitespace, and verify the content-type was application/json.
Wrap JSON.parse in try/catch and log the offending string so the next failure is diagnosable.
tips: JSON.parse(undefined) and JSON.parse('') both throw — guard for empty input.
An API returning an HTML error page is the classic 'Unexpected token <' cause.

guides.title: Track down an unexpected NaN
steps: Remember NaN is contagious: any arithmetic with NaN yields NaN, so find the first place it appears, not the last.
Log each operand just before the math; check types with typeof — a string '12' in subtraction, or undefined, both produce NaN.
Look for parseInt/parseFloat/Number on input that may be empty or non-numeric, which returns NaN.
Check object property access that returned undefined (undefined * 2 is NaN) earlier in the chain.
Add Number.isNaN() guards or default values at the point the value enters the calculation.
Re-run and confirm a real number flows through every step.
tips: Use Number.isNaN(x), not the global isNaN(x) — the global coerces and gives false positives.
NaN === NaN is false; never compare to NaN with ==.

guides.title: Debug a CORS error from the browser
steps: Read the console message precisely — 'No Access-Control-Allow-Origin' is different from a failed preflight (OPTIONS) or a credentials mismatch.
Open the Network tab and inspect the failing request and any preceding OPTIONS preflight; look at the response headers actually returned.
Confirm the server sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin matching your origin (or *), and for non-simple requests, Allow-Methods and Allow-Headers.
If you send cookies/auth, the server must set Allow-Credentials: true AND echo a specific origin (not *), and the client must set credentials: 'include'.
On a Node/Express server, add the cors middleware and configure origin/methods rather than hand-rolling headers.
Reload and verify the preflight returns 204/200 with the right headers and the real request succeeds.
tips: CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server — the request reaches your backend even when the browser blocks the response.
Allow-Origin: * cannot be combined with credentials — you must echo the exact origin.

guides.title: Debug state that won't update / shows a stale value
steps: Confirm you are reading the value after a re-render, not synchronously right after the setter — setState is asynchronous and the local variable stays old.
If the new value depends on the previous one, use the functional updater: setCount(c => c + 1) instead of setCount(count + 1).
Check for a stale closure: an interval/event handler set up once captures the first render's value forever — add the value to the dependency array or use a ref.
Verify you are creating a new object/array, not mutating in place — React skips re-render when the reference is unchanged.
console.log inside the render body (not inside the handler) to see what value the component actually renders with.
Re-run and confirm the UI reflects the latest value.
tips: Multiple setCount(count+1) in one handler all use the same stale count; the functional form fixes batching.
Mutating state (arr.push(x); setArr(arr)) often renders nothing because the reference didn't change.

guides.title: Debug undefined process.env variables
steps: console.log(process.env.MY_VAR) right where you read it to confirm it is undefined and not just falsy.
If using dotenv, ensure require('dotenv').config() runs BEFORE any module that reads the variable — import order matters.
Verify the .env file is in the directory the process starts from and is named exactly .env (not .env.txt).
Check the variable name spelling and case match exactly between .env and code; env names are case-sensitive.
Confirm .env is not gitignored away in the deploy environment — production usually sets vars through the platform, not a file.
Restart the process — env changes are not hot-reloaded.
tips: All process.env values are strings: process.env.DEBUG === 'false' is truthy as a string.
Frontend bundlers only expose vars with a specific prefix (e.g. VITE_, REACT_APP_) — others are stripped.

guides.title: Debug floating-point arithmetic surprises
steps: Recognize the symptom: 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.30000000000000004 because IEEE-754 binary floats cannot represent these decimals exactly.
For comparisons, never use === on computed floats; compare within an epsilon: Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON.
For display, round at the end with toFixed(2) or Intl.NumberFormat — but know toFixed returns a string.
For money, switch to integer cents (multiply by 100, do integer math, divide at the end) or a decimal library.
Check for accumulation: summing many floats compounds error; sum integers where possible.
Re-run and confirm comparisons and totals behave as expected.
tips: toFixed has its own rounding quirks (1.005.toFixed(2) can give '1.00') — integer cents avoid it.
Number.EPSILON only works for numbers near 1.0; scale the epsilon for large magnitudes.

guides.title: Debug an unexpected object/array mutation
steps: Confirm the symptom: a value you didn't touch changed — that means two variables point at the same object/array reference.
Find where the reference was 'copied': const b = a copies the reference, not the contents.
Check functions that mutate in place: sort, reverse, splice, push all change the original array.
Search for the shared reference being handed to a caller and then modified by them.
Make a copy at the boundary: [...arr], {...obj}, structuredClone(obj) for deep, or use non-mutating methods (toSorted, map, filter).
Re-run and confirm the original stays intact.
tips: Spread is a shallow copy; nested objects are still shared — use structuredClone for deep copies.
Array.prototype.sort mutates AND returns the same array, so const sorted = arr.sort() doesn't protect the original.

guides.title: Debug ECONNREFUSED connection failures
steps: Read the host and port from the error (e.g. ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432) — that is what your code tried to reach.
Confirm the target service is actually running and listening on that port (lsof -i :PORT, or the service's own status command).
Check the host: inside Docker, localhost refers to the container itself, not the host — use the service name or host.docker.internal.
Verify the port and credentials in your connection string/env match the service's real config.
Test connectivity independently (curl, telnet, or the DB CLI) to isolate code vs network.
Add a connection retry/backoff if the dependency starts slower than your app (common in compose stacks).
tips: ECONNREFUSED means nothing is listening; a hang/timeout instead usually means a firewall or wrong host.
In docker-compose, services reach each other by service name, not localhost.

guides.title: Debug async race conditions / out-of-order results
steps: Reproduce reliably by logging a timestamp and an identifier at the start and end of each async operation.
Check loops: a forEach with async callbacks does NOT wait — all iterations fire concurrently, so order and 'done' timing are unpredictable.
If you need sequential execution, use a for...of loop with await inside; if you need parallel-but-collected, use await Promise.all(arr.map(...)).
Look for shared mutable state written by concurrent operations — guard or restructure so each task owns its data.
Confirm you await every promise that a later step depends on; an un-awaited write can be read before it lands.
Re-run several times to confirm the order is now deterministic.
tips: await inside forEach is a classic no-op — the loop returns before any callback resolves.
Promise.all rejects on the first failure; use Promise.allSettled when you want all results regardless.

guides.title: Debug a regular expression that won't match
steps: Paste the pattern and a real sample into a tester (regex101) and read the explanation pane to see what each token does.
Check escaping: in a string-built RegExp, backslashes must be doubled ('\\d' for \d); a literal /\d/ does not.
Verify flags: missing g means only the first match; missing i means case-sensitive; missing m changes ^/$ behavior.
Watch greedy quantifiers (.*) that consume too much — switch to lazy (.*?) or a more specific character class.
If reusing a RegExp object with the g flag, beware lastIndex — it advances between .test()/.exec() calls and can skip matches.
Re-test against several inputs, including edge cases, before trusting it.
tips: A global-flag RegExp is stateful; create a fresh one or reset .lastIndex when looping.
Anchors ^ and $ match string ends by default, not line ends — add the m flag for per-line.

guides.title: Debug date/timezone off-by-one bugs
steps: Log the Date object and its .toISOString() side by side to see the UTC value versus the local rendering.
Recognize the common trap: new Date('2024-01-15') parses as UTC midnight, which can display as the previous day in negative-offset zones.
Decide whether you mean a calendar date (no zone) or an instant in time — they need different handling.
For date-only logic, work in UTC consistently (use getUTCDate/setUTCHours or parse with explicit time and Z).
Avoid getMonth() surprises: it is 0-indexed, so January is 0.
Re-test across a couple of timezones (change TZ env var locally) to confirm no off-by-one remains.
tips: '2024-01-15' is UTC, but '2024-01-15T00:00:00' (no Z) is local — that difference causes the off-by-one.
Date getMonth() is 0-based but getDate() is 1-based — easy to mix up.

guides.title: Debug Express middleware/routes that never run
steps: Add a console.log at the top of the middleware/route to confirm whether it is reached at all.
Check ordering: Express runs middleware top-to-bottom; a middleware registered after the route, or after a res.send, never fires.
Confirm the previous middleware calls next() — forgetting next() (and not sending a response) hangs the request.
Verify the HTTP method and path match exactly, including a leading slash and any router mount prefix (app.use('/api', router)).
For body parsing issues, ensure express.json() is registered before routes that read req.body.
Reload and watch the logs to confirm the chain reaches your handler.
tips: A route that sends a response and also calls next() can trigger 'headers already sent'.
app.use('/api', router) means a route '/users' inside the router is actually /api/users.

guides.title: Fix "Cannot set headers after they are sent"
steps: Read the stack to find the second response write — the error fires on the line that runs after a response was already sent.
Search the handler for more than one res.send/res.json/res.end/res.redirect on the same path.
Look for a missing return: after res.json(...), execution continues unless you return, so add return res.json(...).
Check async flows where a callback sends a response and the outer code also sends one after awaiting.
Ensure error handlers don't respond on a request that a try block already answered.
Re-run the request and confirm exactly one response is sent.
tips: if (err) res.status(500).send() without a return will fall through to the success response — add return.
Calling next() after sending a response can also re-enter handlers that respond again.

guides.title: Debug a failing npm install
steps: Read the first error block, not the last — npm prints the root cause near the top before the cleanup noise.
For ERESOLVE peer dependency conflicts, read which package wants which version; align versions or, as a temporary measure, retry with --legacy-peer-deps.
For node-gyp/native build failures, confirm you have the build toolchain (python3, make, a C++ compiler) and a Node version the package supports.
Delete node_modules and package-lock.json and run npm install fresh to clear a corrupt or partial state.
Check your Node/npm versions against the package's engines field; mismatches cause cryptic failures.
Re-run and read the npm-debug log path it prints if it still fails.
tips: --legacy-peer-deps hides the conflict; resolve versions properly before shipping.
Clearing the cache (npm cache clean --force) helps with corrupted-tarball errors.

guides.title: Debug breakpoints that won't hit in Node
steps: Confirm the process started in debug mode: node --inspect-brk app.js, or that your VS Code launch config attaches to the right port (default 9229).
Check you are debugging the file that actually runs — if a bundler/transpiler is involved, breakpoints must be set with source maps enabled.
Verify the code path is reached at all by adding a console.log next to the breakpoint.
Ensure the source on disk matches the running process; a watcher restart or stale build can desync them.
For TypeScript/Babel, confirm sourceMap is on and the debugger maps generated JS back to your source.
Reattach the debugger and confirm it pauses; --inspect-brk pauses on the first line so you can attach in time.
tips: --inspect attaches but does not pause; --inspect-brk pauses immediately so you don't miss early code.
Greyed-out breakpoints in VS Code usually mean missing or wrong source maps.

guides.title: Debug truthy/falsy condition bugs
steps: List the falsy values you might trip on: false, 0, '', null, undefined, NaN — all of these fail an if(x) check.
Identify which value your condition mishandles: if(count) skips a valid 0; if(name) skips a valid empty string.
Replace loose checks with explicit ones: if (x !== undefined), if (x != null) for null-or-undefined, or if (Number.isFinite(x)).
For defaults, prefer ?? (nullish coalescing) over || when 0 or '' are valid values: port = input ?? 3000.
Re-test the edge values (0, '', false) explicitly to confirm they take the intended branch.
Audit nearby conditions for the same trap.
tips: value || default replaces 0 and '' with the default; value ?? default only replaces null/undefined.
if (arr.length) is fine, but if (obj) is true even for an empty {} — check the property you actually mean.

guides.title: Debug a failing fetch() call
steps: Distinguish the failure mode: 'Failed to fetch' (network/CORS/wrong URL, request never completed) versus a completed response with a bad status code.
Remember fetch does NOT reject on HTTP errors — check response.ok and response.status before reading the body.
Log the full URL being requested; a relative URL resolves against the current page and may hit the wrong host.
Open the Network tab (or use a Node debug log) to see the actual request, method, headers, and response.
For Node < 18 there is no global fetch — confirm the runtime version or import a polyfill.
Wrap in try/catch, handle both the network error and the !response.ok case, then re-run.
tips: A 404/500 still resolves the promise — you must check response.ok yourself.
Reading response.json() twice throws 'body already used' — read it once into a variable.

guides.title: Debug unexpected object iteration results
steps: Decide what you want to iterate: own enumerable keys, all keys including inherited, or values.
Replace for...in (which walks the prototype chain) with Object.keys/entries/values for own enumerable properties only.
If you must use for...in, guard each key with Object.hasOwn(obj, key) (or obj.hasOwnProperty) to skip inherited props.
Check that numeric-string keys aren't reordering: integer-like keys are iterated in ascending numeric order, not insertion order.
If you need guaranteed insertion order and arbitrary keys, use a Map instead of a plain object.
Re-run and confirm only the intended keys appear, in the order you expect.
tips: for...in includes inherited enumerable properties — a common source of phantom keys.
Object key order is insertion order EXCEPT integer-like keys, which come first in numeric order.

guides.title: Debug an event handler firing multiple times
steps: Add a console.count in the handler to confirm how many times it actually runs per event.
Check whether addEventListener is called inside code that re-runs (a render, a loop, a re-init) — each call stacks another listener.
Verify you remove old listeners before adding new ones, or attach the listener exactly once at setup.
Note that addEventListener with the same function reference won't duplicate, but a new inline/arrow function each time will — keep a stable reference.
For one-shot needs, use { once: true } so the listener auto-removes after firing.
Re-run and confirm count is 1 per event.
tips: removeEventListener needs the exact same function reference you added — an inline arrow can't be removed.
Re-binding handlers on every React render or framework update is the usual stacking cause.

guides.title: Debug a closure capturing the wrong loop variable
steps: Reproduce: callbacks created in a for loop all report the final value (often the loop's end count) instead of their own iteration's value.
Check the loop declaration: var i is function-scoped, so every closure shares the one i that ended at its final value.
Change var to let in the loop header — let creates a fresh binding per iteration, giving each closure its own value.
If you can't use let, wrap the body in an IIFE that takes i as an argument to capture it by value.
Confirm any setTimeout/event callback inside the loop now sees its own iteration value.
Re-run and verify each callback reports the correct per-iteration value.
tips: for (let i...) is the modern fix; for (var i...) shares a single binding across all iterations.
Array methods like forEach already give each iteration its own scope — the bug is specific to var in C-style loops.

guides.title: Debug a Node process that exits before async work finishes
steps: Confirm the symptom: logs or writes after an await never appear because the process ended first.
Check the top-level structure — if your async work is in a function that is called but not awaited, nothing keeps the event loop alive.
Wrap top-level async logic in an async main() and await it, or use top-level await in an ESM module.
Look for an explicit process.exit() that runs before pending promises resolve — it terminates immediately, flushing nothing.
Ensure any open handles (DB pools, servers) that you rely on aren't closed prematurely in a finally that runs too early.
Re-run and confirm all expected output appears before exit.
tips: process.exit() does not wait for pending async work or buffered stdout — avoid it for clean shutdowns.
Node exits when the event loop is empty; an un-awaited promise does not keep it alive.

guides.title: Resolving a merge conflict
steps: Run `git status` to list the files marked as 'both modified' — those are your conflicts.
Open each conflicted file and find the `<<<<<<< HEAD`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>` marker blocks.
Edit the region to the final code you want, deleting all three marker lines completely.
Run `git add <file>` on each resolved file to mark the conflict as settled.
When `git status` shows no remaining conflicts, run `git commit` to finish the merge.
Verify nothing broke by building/testing before you push.
tips: Use `git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U` to list only the unresolved files.
If you make a mess, `git merge --abort` puts you back exactly where you started.
`git checkout --theirs <file>` / `--ours <file>` takes one whole side if you don't want to hand-merge.

guides.title: Undoing your last commit
steps: Decide whether you want to keep the changes (most common) or throw them away.
To keep the changes but undo the commit, run `git reset --soft HEAD~1` — the files stay staged.
To keep the changes unstaged in your working tree, run `git reset --mixed HEAD~1` (the default).
To discard the commit AND its changes entirely, run `git reset --hard HEAD~1`.
Run `git status` and `git log --oneline -3` to confirm the history looks right.
If the commit was already pushed, use `git revert HEAD` instead to add an undo-commit safely.
tips: Never `reset --hard` a commit you already pushed to a shared branch — it rewrites public history.
Even after `reset --hard`, the old commit lives in `git reflog` for ~30 days so it's recoverable.

guides.title: Recovering a lost commit with reflog
steps: Run `git reflog` to see every position HEAD has pointed to, newest first.
Scan the list for the commit you lost — look at the messages and `HEAD@{n}` labels.
Copy the short SHA of the commit you want back.
Create a branch at it with `git branch recovered <sha>` (safest) or `git checkout <sha>`.
Inspect `git log recovered` to confirm it's the right snapshot.
Merge or cherry-pick it back into your working branch as needed.
tips: Reflog is local-only — it won't help recover work from another machine.
Entries expire (90 days reachable, 30 unreachable by default), so recover sooner rather than later.
`git reflog show <branch>` scopes the log to one branch's tip movements.

guides.title: Getting out of detached HEAD state
steps: Run `git status` — the top line will say 'HEAD detached at <sha>'.
Decide if you made commits while detached: run `git log --oneline -5` to check.
If you have commits to keep, create a branch right where you are: `git branch -c keep-work` then `git switch keep-work`.
If you have nothing to keep, just `git switch main` (or your branch) to reattach.
Confirm with `git status` that you're now 'On branch <name>'.
If you abandoned commits accidentally, find them again in `git reflog`.
tips: Detached HEAD isn't an error — it's normal when you check out a specific SHA or tag.
Commits made in detached HEAD are orphaned if you switch away without branching them.

guides.title: Discarding uncommitted local changes
steps: Run `git status` to see what's modified and whether changes are staged or not.
To discard changes in one tracked file, run `git restore <file>` (or `git checkout -- <file>` on old Git).
To unstage but keep edits, run `git restore --staged <file>`.
To wipe ALL tracked-file changes, run `git restore .` from the repo root.
To also delete new untracked files, run `git clean -n` first (dry run), then `git clean -fd`.
Confirm with `git status` that the tree is clean.
tips: `git clean -fd` is irreversible — those files were never tracked, so reflog can't save them.
Always run `git clean -n` (dry run) before `-f` to see exactly what will be deleted.

guides.title: Moving a commit to the correct branch
steps: While still on the wrong branch, note the commit SHA with `git log --oneline -1`.
Create or switch to the correct branch: `git switch -c right-branch` (branches from here).
